speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. I understand a radio broadcast heard over certain stations at noon to-day carried the

Mobilization Act

news that arrests had been made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of certain officials in Toronto under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. I shojild be glad if the minister would make a statement to the house, so that we may be informed of the latest developments in this connection.

Mr. Speaker, prior to receiving notice of the hon. member's question I had a statement prepared with regard to this matter. It is as follows:
I feel that hon. members should be informed that this morning the divisional registrar of the mobilization division with headquarters at Toronto was arrested together with several others not connected with this or any other government department. The prosecution is in the hands of the Department of Justice. I am informed that the charge is laid under section 31 of the mobilization regulations-that is, doing an act likely to nullify or impede the operation of the regulations or aiding and abetting the person committing such an act. One of the inspectors of the mobilization section has been appointed acting registrar.	The investigation has not implicated anyone else in the service.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, July 5, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley -Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Flax fibre administrator - administration, $30,500.
How much flax was handled by this administrator, and what are the stocks at present on hand?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to fibre flax?
Yes.

The only flax on hand is that not processed; they are working at the job all the time. During 1942 there was a fur-

War Appropriation-Agriculture
ther expansion of acreage of some 2,500 acres, and three more mills commenced operations. The expansion of the industry is indicated in the following table:
1939 8 mills
8,300 acres 1,344 tons $837,000
1942 38 mills 47,000 acres 8,730 tons, estimated $3,202,000
During the year sixteen mills operated in Ontario and twenty-two in Quebec.

Item agreed to.
Fertilizers and pesticides administrator- administration, $31,600.
Fertilizers subventions and freight allowances,

I should like to discuss a matter which I have taken up before with the minister. This time I am not in a critical mood, although I may be later in the day. Of the domestic corn produced in our province some eighty-five per cent is recovered in the form of ensilage. As the minister knows, the fertilizer subsidy does not apply to domestic com. The farmers have been asked to increase the production of dairy products and it is felt that this subsidy should apply to this class of corn. I would ask that the minister have his department give consideration to this matter. I understand that some of tne officials of the department in British Co'umbia have agreed with our estimate that we recover that percentage for dairy feed.

We should like to give a subsidy on corn, but unfortunately this year we have had to withdraw it from all com. The reason is that we are short of fertilizers and we have to distribute them largely in connection with grass and other grain crops.

Item agreed to.
Seeds administrator-administration, $16,500.
Joint seed programme-1941, $180,000.
Does this item cover vegetable seeds or grain seeds generally?
It covers stock seeds, alfalfa seed, red clover seed, oil bearing seed and seeds of that type, not only for Canada but those that are sent to Great Britain.
Was there any surplus of alfalfa seed this year for export?
There was some for export last year and there will be some for export this year, but the amount will be somewhat limited.
How much was exported last year? If the minister has the figures, I should like to know what percentage came from western grain.

A total of 660,000 pounds of western seed was moved east, including approximately 357,000 pounds which was purchased by the board at not more than 33 cents per pound. On this latter quantity the government paid storage and transportation costs to eastern Canada in order that the seed could be distributed under the established ceiling prices.

Item agreed to.
Bacon board-administration, $71,300.
How many members are there on this board and how many employees, are there?
There are six members of the board, and either four or five employees. I have not the names here at the moment. Then there is an advisory committee.
How often does this board meet?

The full board meets about onoe a month and sometimes more than that, but the manager, Mr. Pearsall, who is an official of the department, is constantly at work in connection with the activities of the board.
I understand that the bacon board has now become the meat board; has there been any increase in the number of the board?
There has not been any increase, and we have not in mind the making of any.

This morning in the committee we listened to a member of this board, and we were given to understand that the board is buying beef at a lower price during the coming year. Can the minister enlarge upon that statement?

As all members know, we are under price control, and so far as beef is concerned there is a selling price established of between 20 and 21 cents a pound for complete carcasses at Toronto. A flat ceiling on beef cuts is established throughout the year, and then from May 27 on to some time in the middle of August there is a floor established which is a quarter-cent below the ceiling. This gradually goes down until in October it is two and one-quarter cents below the ceiling. That is on the cuts of beef, not on the carcass. There is a floor price on the cuts which is a quarter-cent below the ceiling for the period through which we are now passing. This spread goes down to two and a half cents at the period at which the original ceiling prices were set, during September and

War Appropriation-Agriculture
October. Then it starts to rise again until in the spring it is back up to within a quarter of a cent of the ceiling on cuts.
The result is that on live cattle there could be a spread at the widest point of about a cent a pound; that is, it could drop about a cent below the ceiling. We have an understanding that we will buy when cattle get down to that floor. These cattle are bought to take care of. any deficiencies in the country outside of the area where they are bought. After the supply in Canada has been taken care of, we have an undertaking to supply any surplus beef to Britain. That beef must be frozen. If we buy that beef it would have to be put into freezers and frozen and eventually shipped to Britain.

I think it would be well if the minister made clear to the house now that there is no guaranteed price to the producers, that the guarantee is only to the packer and that the producer is at the mercy of the market.

No. If the hon. member follows through what I have just been saying he will note that there cannot be any great spread which will accrue to the packer. We begin to buy beef when it gets down to the floor and see to it that that beef goes into freezers for shipment for Britain.

The evidence given before the agriculture committee was that the government buys beefs only from the packer, that the price on the open market could drop as much as five cents a pound and the government would not purchase beef on the market, that they would only purchase from the packers at a given floor. There is no guarantee at all so far as the price on the open market is concerned.

There is probably some misunderstanding of the evidence. The board has the power to purchase beef and order it into packing plants and order it processed for the British market. We only buy beef, to be put into packing plants where it can be frozen. There is authority to see that that beef goes into freezers. The practical way of doing it, unless someone is trying to get a greater margin of profit than he is entitled to, would be simply to order the packing plants under certain circumstances to deliver a certain proportion of the purchases into the freezers. If there is any difficulty about it there is sufficient authority under the orders in council to permit of its being handled otherwise.

What we want to
know is whether that authority is being used. Will the minister tell the committee by what

sort of organization the beef feeders in a given area can sell their beef to a government agent in case they are unable to sell it on the open market at the price they should get?

I can assure all members of the committee that if it ever becomes necessary to use the authority we have we shall use it, but as long as we can carry on through the ordinary channels of trade, if that is not to the disadvantage of the producer or the consumer, we shall carry on in that way. But if we ever have reason to exercise our authority we will use it.
What would constitute such reason?

If, for instance, there
were no buyers on a certain market and the price were allowed to go down, we would probably ask somebody to buy.

Suppose the buyers
were refusing to pay the price they should pay?

That would be exactly
the reason why we would take action. We have authority under those conditions to take
action and secure the beef.

Suppose the farmers
find the prices are too low; to whom can they apply in Alberta, for instance?

There are different
ways of doing it. We can buy the cattle and notify the producer to ship them to certain plants to be slaughtered under our direction, or the government can secure them outright and have them sent to the plant. We have the authority to do anything that it is necessary to do, but we are not looking for trouble. If somebody creates trouble we will take action,

The trouble is that
the Department of Agriculture has overlooked a serious situation. I have a letter here from a stock breeders association that fed 1,000 head last year, and the writer declares that out of approximately 1,000 head of cattle fed by the association not one brought as much as 12 cents, while many sold for 10J and 10{ cents.

On what market was
that?

This is from the
stock breeders association at Cardston. It does not say where they were selling, but they were unable to get government assistance. What I want to know is how they can get government assistance in a case of that kind.

War Appropriation-Agriculture
They could wire to the department, or the hon. member could bring his wire to the department and the officials would act if action were warranted.

I turned over the
wire I received from that organization about June 9 or 10, so that there was every opportunity for the department to take action.

That was the same
wire that was referred to on a previous occasion?
Yes.

I think that was acted
on.

It is an indication
that all was not well, and if the minister had authority to act and did not use it I want to know what can be done in a similar case.

All I can say to the
hon. member is that the market has not been going down. It has been rising, and surprising many people by rising over a considerable time. I think the situation can well be left to the kind of cattle dealers I know in the vicinity my hon. friend speaks of, who know the cattle business better than anybody else in Canada. As long as the price is keeping tip or remaining at a dead level on the regular market, I think they can be trusted to sell their cattle at a fair price.

There are very few
people who know more about cattle than the people who have written me.

That is exactly what
I was saying.
And they were not able to get a price. That indicates that something is wrong.
The price was there on the market.

Will the minister explain why the market is advancing so rapidly? This morning's Globe and Mail says it has advanced forty cents a hundred. Why is it advancing so rapidly, in view of the announcement that the price will shortly be dropped one cent?

It is difficult to understand. Here we have one member telling us that a man cannot sell his cattle at a reasonable price, and another saying that prices are going up forty cents a hundred. There is something wrong somewhere between those two statements.

Exactly, and we want to have it corrected. There must be something
wrong with the government's machinery. The people selling beef have no recourse in case the price is low.

There is something
wrong, I think, with the report. I think that statement came at the end of a certain meeting. I think cattle have been marketed fairly successfully since then. We have had no further complaint that I know of from these people.

A return which was brought down the other day showed that the Department of Munitions and Supply was buying beef for the armed forces above the ceiling price. If that department can buy at a price above the ceiling for the armed forces, it will readily be seen what a difficulty that creates. What liaison is there between the Department of Agriculture and the prices board in order to govern that situation?

There are two officers of the Department of Agriculture on the board. The manager of the meat board is also a member of the staff of the department. The Department of Munitions and Supply for many weeks now have been paying the ceiling price and not more than the ceiling price for beef.

Item agreed to.
Dairy products board-administration, $14,950.

I should like to say a word on this item, which the minister can pass very quickly if he will answer a question; then we may spend a couple of hours on the next item. I want to know how the subsidy paid on dairy products is arrived at. I have been trying to get this information for the last two weeks in the agriculture committee but so far have not succeeded. I presume it is not within the knowledge of the officials who have been there. How do they arrive at a set price on dairy products such as fluid milk? What is taken into account? Is the tax paid on land taken into account, the value of the land, the amount of wages paid, and other considerations in arriving at these subsidies?

Very early in the war the prices of dairy products were quite low. Butter was around 20 cents, cheese around 10 or 12 cents, and milk was about $1.60, but now prices are very much higher than that. The ceiling price on butter is 35 cents and the floor is 32 cents, and there is a subsidy on top of that of eight cents in the summer and ten cents in the winter. On cheese the price is slightly over 20 cents and on milk it runs from $1.85 to $2.50.
With regard to production, costs of course are different in different places, and I can

War Appropriation-Agriculture
only say that we were told by representatives of the dairy industry, very early in the war and again no longer than eighteen months ago, that prices very much lower than the prices being paid now would cover cost of production. In fact, it was suggested that if prices were established very much lower than the prices we have now for the whole war the industry would be well taken care of. We did not establish those prices early in the war and therefore I can see that the dairy people would now be justified in asking for more than actual cost of production in order to balance some of the earnings of the present period against the period when we were under cost of production.
I recite these facts to show that some attention has been given to cost of production. We did attempt to get a price higher than we had been assured earlier in the war would cover cost of production, and we have prices considerably higher than that, believing that the farmers were entitled to more than cost of production because they took less for a time.
So far as recent arrangements are concerned, the dairy industry was consulted and the whole matter was discussed with them, both by the prices board and by representatives of the Department of Agriculture before the present subsidies, which are paid on top of the price, were provided; and we thought at the time we put them on that everyone was satisfied. We found afterwards, however, that there were some who were not entirely satisfied with the arrangement made, though we have considered the arrangement fairly satisfactory and we are abiding by it.

If these agriculture estimates were rushed through as they stand they would form interesting reading for the farmers. I appreciate the explanation the minister has given and I have been told by farm members from Ontario that they are satisfied with these particular prices. In British Columbia, as the minister knows, we are not satisfied. The deputy minister of agriculture, in his evidence, admitted that we had an exceptional situation in that province and that our costs were higher. The department has taken into consideration to a certain extent the question of cost of production. The minister has pointed out that the price of milk varies in different cities. I presume therefore he admits that it costs more to produce in certain areas than in others. This factor has not been taken into account so far as British Columbia is concerned.
I am not satisfied with the minister's answer. I should like to know who advised

that farmers were satisfied with the prices that have been settled. In arriving at the subsidy, did the department assume that there is a difference in the quality of milk used for evaporated milk and in the fluid market respectively? In other words, one farm produces two ten-gallon cans of milk, ten gallons going to the fluid market and ten into the evaporated milk trade, both standard milk. Is there any difference in the quality? We do not think so. I should like to know whether the minister is of the opinion that there is a difference in the quality. When he answers that question I will ask another.

Of course, the hon.
member, who is familiar with the dairy farming industry and also with the processing of milk, will understand that there are different conditions across Canada; that is to say, there are different requirements at different places for the delivery of milk. Whole milk is delivered in cities or towns of much smaller size and in certain areas costs have to be higher. They have to be higher in a large city than in smaller places. That accounts for some of the variations between the ceiling that may be placed and the subsidy that is established in some particular community. As regards the prices of processed milk as compared with whole milk, the lower price paid for processed milk is accounted for by the fact that there is a smaller demand for the canned milk in these particular communities than there is for whole milk. Whole milk is delivered, or was delivered before the war started, in some provinces, though not in British Columbia, under the direction of a milk board appointed provincially. That milk board dealt with the situation within the province. Quite often they established proportions of milk to be delivered by different suppliers. A certain percentage was to be delivered as whole milk and that was all that could be distributed as whole milk. The object was to distribute the business over the suppliers, and any milk outside that particular pool was sold at a different price. Much of that milk went into canning factories, into cheese or butter or something else. I do not believe that there was a board at that time in British Columbia, and there is not now; *nevertheless the situation there is governed by the same consideration. There is a demand for a very considerable amount of whole milk in cities the size of Vancouver and Victoria, and that demand itself creates a price for whole milk. I am sure, however, it will be agreed that if the canning plants in British Columbia were to be asked to pay that same price for whole milk they would not be able to compete with canning factories elsewhere;

War Appropriation-Agriculture
and much of this milk is sold not in the local community but in the general market outside. I understand there has been some difficulty in British Columbia because of the two prices paid for milk, one going into the canning plants and the other for use as whole milk.

It is quite true that we are not operating under a board similar to those established in other .provinces. The marketing act, so far, has proved .profitable only to the legal profession. It has been to the privy council half a dozen times. Seventy per cent of our farmers sell their milk in competition with the lower-priced milk .products of Ontario-because the deputy minister has admitted that milk can be produced at lower cost in Ontario and Quebec than in British Columbia-and all of the remaining thirty per cent of the farmers in British Columbia market their .milk on the fluid markets, yet by their very regulations, laid down not by the minister's department but in the holy of holies over here, we are compelled to pay our own farmers the .prices they set for the fluid milk. In other words, we have our own wholesale plant and we are forced to pay to our wholesale .plant the price they set for our producers. Unfortunately, the wartime prices board always consults the minority, and never the majority, when it comes to British Columbia, and so they compel us to pay to the retail trade the price they set for our own producers, which means the price that the minority or independent shipper wants to meet. We cannot see that there is any difference in the quality of milk and there should be no difference in the price.
The minister admitted the other day, indirectly at any rate, that there is a difference in the quality of milk produced. May I point out that the three maritime provinces and British Columbia are the only provinces which are entirely tuberculosis-free areas. I am including the maritime provinces; it is an honour to them. Our milk is therefore of a higher quality. We cannot see how the amount of subsidy is arrived at by the board, which we understand sets the price paid to the farmer, subject to approval by the wartime prices board. I understand the agriculture board sets the amount of the subsidy to be paid.

May I correct that at once. All prices are set by the prices board. Our board does not set prices, but the prices board does. That board, however, does discuss the matter of price with our food board. If we are not satisfied with a price when it is set, if we are not satisfied that the price will get the production we want, then we arrange for the subsidy. That goes on in addition to the price.

In other words, they set the ceiling price, and your department arranges whatever subsidy is necessary. I am thinking about our evaporated milk. We did not particularly complain when you left it on in the summer months before. So far as I can understand from any witness down before the agriculture committee, the main reason of the subsidy is the incentive to increase production. So far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned the Fraser valley is admittedly a deficiency area for milk. I shall have quite a bit to say a little later about its being a deficiency area for potatoes. If the milk subsidy is put on for that reason, we think that that spread should go over on evaporated milk. It is admitted by departmental officials, either the deputy minister or one of the senior officials who appeared before us, that the cost of production in our province is a great deal higher than in any other part of Canada. This statement appears in evidence given before one of the committees. I would urge upon the minister that he take into consideration payment on the quality of milk, and bear in mind the cost of production in making recommendation of the subsidy. I say this with all due deference to the statements of his official, and I should like to know from the minister now which official stated that the price was satisfactory to the dairy farmers of Canada, and who recommended him.
What I stated was that we held meetings with officials of the dairy organizations across Canada-the Dairy Association of Canada, I think is, the name of it-* and we thought we were satisfying them.
That is different.

But I stated that afterwards we found out that some of them were not entirely satisfied, but that we had checked any dissatisfactions which were announced to us, and had satisfied ourselves that the arrangement should remain as it is for this season.
With regard to canned milk and whole milk in British Columbia, we have not been asking for canned milk from British Columbia, and that is one of the difficulties in connection with two or three of these products that are being discussed. I repeat that we have not asked British Columbia to supply us with canned milk. We would very much prefer that British Columbia should entirely take care of the local situation on the western side of Canada with regard to milk. In other words, we are not bidding for the milk of British Columbia. We quite admit that if we were, we would probably have to bid a higher price than we would for milk from some other places. But the supply which we wish

War Appropriation-Agriculture
to send out of Canada we are obtaining at a lesser cost, where the freight rate is yery much lower than if we shipped from British Columbia. I admit that that is not a complete answer. Some consideration should be given to British Columbia because of its location, because of the fact that freights from there are higher, and I think that; some consideration has been given, although perhaps not enough, to that fact.
Did the minister say that we should look after the fluid milk?
I said that we would like you to.

I should like that statement explained a little. Are we not looking after it now? I should like to know where you are getting any milk in the province of British Columbia if that province does not produce for its fluid milk market. Surely that is not what the minister meant.

I meant just exactly what I said, that we are not anxious to get milk from British Columbia canned; we would very much prefer that British Columbia dispose of their milk as whole milk or butter rather than have it canned, and therefore we are not bidding up the price of canned milk to the price of fluid milk.

Surely the minister will admit that any dairy country, even Ontario, must have some place to dispose of its milk. You cannot in any dairy country or any dairy district dispose of all your milk on the fluid market. The minister knows that a certain percentage of it must be put in byproducts-cheese, butter or evaporated milk- and obviously, with your fresh season and then your off season, you cannot sell all your milk in the fluid market in any dairying district. But last year 550,000 cases of evaporated milk were taken from British Columbia. Does anyone think that a dairy district can arrange to provide 550,000 cases of evaporated milk for the British market, which needed it so badly, in one year, and in the next year put all its milk on to the fluid or some other market?
May I ask a question? It is directed to the hon. member for Fraser Valley.
I do not have to be a witness, but I shall be glad to answer it.

My question is this.
Fraser Valley has been represented in this house as one of the most fertile spots in the universe. Can the hon. member enlighten us on this point: why should the cost of pro-

duotion be so much higher in such a productive, fertile spot than in our raviney knolls and sandy hills down in Ontario?

We can explain that. It is very easily explained. There are perhaps two
or three reasons. First of all you must bear in mind that in British Columbia, in the lower Fraser valley, land, clearing operations are very expensive. I do not think you can put under cultivation from the virgin forest in the Fraser valley one acre of land under $500 an acre. That is the first cause. Then' we in British Columbia, industrially at least, have been more generous with our workers and have paid them more highly than any other province in Canada. We have led in social legislation, with the result that the costs have gone up. We have areas of very productive land which are kept productive only because they are under a diking system; they are alluvial land, and some of our farmers are paying on this account up to $7.50 per acre. Let anybody take the most highly taxed land in Ontario and ask the farmers there how they would like to pay $7.50 an acre in taxation. These are some of the factors which require that we in British Columbia should get a higher price than other provinces.

I do not desire to enter into any controversy between Ontario farmers and British Columbia farmers, dairy or otherwise. But I understood the hon. member for Fraser Valley to say that the milk in British Columbia is of a higher quality because they are in an accredited area. That, I believe, pertains to the whole province. But I am sure that we in Ontario have a very much higher number of fully accredited herds of dairy cattle than any other part of the dominion. So that I think, taking it by and large, it cannot be established that milk is of a higher quality in one part of Canada than in another.
I have not said that our milk is of a higher quality throughout, but the hon. member has borne out exactly what I said, and if he lives in an accredited area-
I do.

-he will know that his cattle cost more and are worth more than those in a non-accredited area. That is one of the points which I am glad he brought out. It hurts British Columbia members who are trying to get an increase in the price of their dairy products-and their potatoes, to which I shall refer in a minute-when apparently in some parts of Canada, certainly in

War Appropriation-Agriculture
Ontario, hon. members are satisfied with prices; and I do not think it helps much when they cannot even stay and take it when we show that we are not satisfied with their statements.
I want to revert for a minute to the question of our costs, and repeat what the hon. member for New Westminster said about the diking areas. Not only that, but we have to pay up to 12.50 an acre drainage tax as well. On top of that, we have no industries out there, so that we cannot sell our milk in markets where plants which are subsidized by the government will pay a higher price for milk.

I wish to ask the minister if he would elaborate a little further the statement he made a moment ago, that the ceiling price of butter was 35 cents a pound and the floor 32 cents, with a ten-cent and an eight-cent subsidy. I assume that that subsidy goes to the farmer or to the milk producer. What I am interested in is the cost of the butter to the consumer. If your ceiling price is 35 cents a pound I suppose that for eastern Canada that is fixed as per Montreal. I do not know what the cost of butter in eastern Canada is at the present time, but I know that a year ago it was selling for 53 and 55 cents a pound. Now that you have a ceiling of 35 cents, and you are subsidizing the farmer to take up the extra cost to the extent that you have mentioned, why should that butter be retailed to the consumer at 55 and 53 cents a pound? Somebody is crashing the ceiling, or I do not understand the situation.

The position is that the ceiling is 35 cents, as I stated. The floor in May is 32 cents, and the floor advances three-eighths of a cent each month; at present it is 32 3/4 cents, and the price of butter at present is around 33 cents or a little higher. The price has been running about 33 cents for some time. What happens is that as soon as the creamery reports to the government that it has paid the eight-cent subsidy on butter fat-not on pounds of butter-to the farmer, the government reimburses it for the amount it pays to the farmer. It is of course clear from that that the money goes to the producer. The wholesale selling price is 35 cents at Montreal and 36 cents in the maritimes. The base figure is on Montreal, and then it is lower in the west and higher in the east. So that the wholesale price of butter in the maritimes ought to be based on that 36 cents-I am not speaking about the retail price.
Plus the eight cents?
No; the eight cents is paid to the farmers.
But it puts the price of butter up by eight cents?

No, not to the man who purchases it from a store. That is the reason for doing this. We pay the farmer a subsidy of eight cents so that the merchant does not have to charge the consumer a higher price. The idea is to keep down the cost of living. We pay to the producer, and that is not supposed to be passed on to the consumer. The producer gets it.
Is there any control over the price at which the retailer must sell it?
Yes, and I believe that prosecutions are being lodged regularly where people have broken the ceiling regulations.

What protection has the producer of dairy products in respect of grades given by creameries, or by those who buy cream or eggs? Some time ago by government action the price of cream went up. It just happened that at that time I was in a certain section of the country where I received no end of complaints to the effect that the very moment the price went up their grades came down. Of course they blamed the creameries. I tried to get some information, but the information I received in my view was absurd- although it might not have been. I was told that on account of the heavy rains last year the growth of weeds had been prolific, and that the dairy cows had been eating weeds, with the result that the grade of cream came down. The peculiar thing however was that when the price went up the cows were eating weeds in the pasture. About that time I happened to be reading a newspaper in which I came across a small advertisement which read in this way, "Eggs and cream wanted; honest grades; quick return." I will not give the name of the dairy, but the fact that they advertised the giving of honest grades would seem to indicate that somewhere in the picture there may be some dishonest grades. What protection have the producers of dairy products when it comes to grading? They have no way of grading their own cream or eggs. They are at the mercy of those to whom they must sell. Are they sure they will get honest grades?

I am surprised to learn that the difficulties described exist in Alberta. The simple explanation is that the inspection of cream is carried on entirely by provincial authorities. They appoint inspectors. There is an inspector who inspects every plant. I believe under the Alberta legislation-and this is not true in some other places-the plant itself indirectly pays the salary of the inspector who does the grading. But I should not think



War Appropriation-Agriculture
that that would result in there being any improper grading. I believe the provincial authorities in all the provinces take very good care to check carefully the grading of cream. I understand the system in Alberta is fairly complete, and if there is anything wrong with the grading in that province then that is the authority to which the hon. member should appeal.
The minister is assuming that the section of the country I was in was Alberta. I did not say so.
Well, all I can say is that it might be better if it were anywhere else in the west.
The minister mentioned that he would give some information with respect to cheese. Is he prepared to do that now?

When the hon. member was speaking a few moments ago he referred to stock figures as of July 1. The figures I had intended to read, but which I shall not read unless the hon. member so desires, were those to the end of May. The stock figures as of July 1 are these: Total stock, based on nine cities across Canada, on July 1, 1942, amounted to 39,695,000 pounds. On July 1, 1943, it is 24,571,000 pounds. Those are the totals of stocks in store. There is about 15,000,000 pounds less in store this year than on July 1 a year ago. I gave figures to the house the other day which indicate that exports are still higher 'this year than they were a year ago, indicating that up to date we are pretty well keeping up in our deliveries to Great Britain, under contract. We have no intention of changing the cheese price this year; we intend to go through the season on that cheese price.

The figures given by the minister last week, as reported at page 4313 of Hansard, indicate that the production of cheese in the period of January to May, 1943, as compared with the same period in 1942, was down to the extent of fifty per cent, or
52.000.	000 pounds to 26,000,000 pounds. The minister has just stated that cheese in storage amounts to 15,000,000 pounds. When we look at the exports we find that exports for 1943 as compared with those of 1942 are up by only
6.000.	000 pounds. Will the minister explain where the extra quantity of cheese is coming from to fill the quota?
Part of it comes from the surplus carried through from last year.
But, from now on, what is it?

I shall come to that in a moment. Part of what is contained in the
extra exports which have gone overseas, up to date, came out of surpluses carried over from last year, and1 we knew about that when we were setting the position for this year. The position we took at the beginning of the season was that we wanted a certain distribution of milk in order to get the result we had undertaken, whether for the home market or for the British market. We took certain action very early in the season, and announced it, in the hope that we would get a certain amount of cheese for the British market, a certain amount of whole milk for our own market, and a certain amount of butter for our own market. The present position is that in the week ending July 3, 1943, as compared with the similar week in 1942, in western Ontario-the region west of Toronto-we had 7,513 boxes inspected, and in 1942 we had 8,575. That is a decrease of 12-4 per cent in western Ontario as compared with the same week in the same area last year. In Ontario east of Toronto the total this year is 40,998 boxes, and last year it amounted to 42,841 boxes, the decrease being only 4-3 per cent. In other words, as I have stated before, this was a backward season in the early weeks. It was suggested that as the season advanced we would gradually overtake our production of last year. In eastern Ontario we have nearly reached our production of last year; in the last week for which we have figures we are down only 4-3 per cent. In Quebec we are down 25-6 per cent, the production being 21,863 boxes for that week as compared with 29,529 boxes a year ago. The total reduction for that week in Ontario and Quebec amounts to 13-5 per cent. The cumulative position at the end of this period last year was 643,000 boxes as compared with 386,000 boxes this year. That is the total production from April 1, the beginning of the cheese year. This year for this period we are down 39-9 per cent. That is about as near as I can come to the position. By taking all the cheese that is coming onto the market and by taking the carry-over from last year, we have been making the exports of which I have spoken.

The minister has given the
figures up to the first week in July. Does he feel that we are going to be able to meet our quota and still have cheese left for Canada?

We have not yet reached our peak. It is impossible to say definitely whether we will reach it, but we are going to come near enough to reaching it to reach the position we expected to reach at the beginning of the season.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

Is not June usually the
peak?

Everyone knows that
we are about a month late this year because of the backward season.

Did the minister mean a
moment ago that there is not going to be any adjustment in the price of cheese for 1943?

I should think the fact that we have come up to what is usually the peak period without making any adjustment would be the answer to that. But I have stated definitely that we are not going to make any change.

I think the minister or those who are responsible for setting the prices of dairy products in this country should give some consideration to the amount of labour that is put into dairy production. This has been a rather unusual season and I do not expect that the production of dairy products will continue to rise. After all, weather conditions have a considerable bearing upon the production we expect to get from our dairy herds. I do not think the minister is quite within his rights to be so resolute and to say that he does not expect to increase the price. Monetary reward should not always be the consideration, but when we consider that Ontario is going to have only half a crop at best, we must realize that there will be many farmers who will have to buy grain. It is only reasonable to expect that there will be a decrease in dairy production because of that. There are farmers who are well enough off to be able to go out and buy a carload of western grain and thus keep up the production of their herds, but there are many others, and I think they are in the majority, who will not be able to do that. The minister would be wise to keep the present weather conditions in mind. As a practical farmer I do not expect that we shall be able to fulfil our quota of dairy products. Some will have to go without certain things they expect to get if we are to fulfil our agreement with our friends, and I am in favour of doing that. Dairying is an every-day job and it takes a lot of stamina for a man to milk his cows twice a day, seven days a week, three hundred and sixty-five days in the year. We have been somewhat concerned at the number of dairy cattle being sold in the United States. I realize that this is a lucrative market for live stock-
Mr. BLACIvMORE: Will the hon. member tell us why these cattle are going across to the United States?
72537-278i

The United States market is very good at the present time. These people are coming over to Canada and offering extreme prices for dairy cattle, prices not warranted by the ability of the cattle to produce. Many farmers faced with the shortage of labour are selling their surplus cattle, cashing in, as it were. It is a dollars and cents proposition.
Prices must be much better in the United States.

Another reason is the fact that the dairy farmer or live stock producer in Canada turns out a better product than the man in the United States. They come over here to buy cattle in order to keep up the standards of their herds. With the prices they are willing to pay for cattle the average farmer is tempted to sell. Many men are short of help, and this is a lucrative market. But in my opinion this is one thing that will impair the production of dairy products in this country. With the weather conditions we have had, with the shortage of labour we are faced with, I think the minister should keep in mind the fact that there is likely to be an impairment of production.

For the week ending June 24, 1943, there were 516 daily cattle exported to the United States; the exports for the same week in 1942 were 463, a difference of about 53. From January 1 to June 24, 1943, the exports amounted to 19,878 cattle; in the same period in, 1,942 they were 10,341, a difference of 9,537 for the period. However, in spite of the fact that we have exported that number of cattle, we have more cows in Canada to-iday than we have ever had before, four million in round figures. We are shipping cows to the United States in greater numbers to-day than we were before because prices are better. That is all to the good so far as the farmer who is going to sell is concerned. While he is selling cows, there are actually more cows being kept by the whole group of farmers than ever before. I am not going to take individual cases. As has been said many times during this session, there are many farmers of seventy years of age and over who are taking advantage of the higher prices to sell their farms. Some of them are selling their live stock, breeding stock or whatever they may have. Some of this is distributed to other farmers in the community, but some goes across the line. Buyers are continually trying to pick up cows to take to the other side of the line, all of which I think is to the good. This is the one thing that is left to the farmer to sell freely in the United States at a good price. I hope
War Appropriation-Agriculture

that hon. (members are not going to take the [DOT]position that it should not be permitted. So far as I am concerned I am not going to prevent him from doing it. If he can raise cows and calves and sell them in the United States for more money than he can get in Canada, I hope he will keep right on selling them as long as the farmers as a whole keep as many cows as were kept before. That is what they are doing.
The figures on cheese have not given the picture so far as dairying is concerned. We started out in 1936 to try to get our production of cheese up to 200,000,000 pounds in a year. Last year we passed that figure. We did not start that since the war began; we started it the first year I was in the department, in 1936. We advertised for it, we put out a programme and we got up the production even before the war started. Since the war started we have been able to increase it even more, until last year we had double the production of cheese that we had in 1935, or a little more than double. Then when we got our production doubled we were told by the people to whom we were supplying the cheese that they were not at all sure they wanted to take it all. It was not our intention under those conditions to ask the farmer for a large increase in cheese, and we asked him to produce the same amount of cheese as he produced last year. We told the British we would do all we could to get them 150,000,000 pounds. Last year we told them we would do all we could to get them 125,000,000 pounds, and before we got them that amount they suggested we might ease up. We have to consider our own farmers as well as others, even when we are at war. We suggested that this year we would do the best we could do to get them
150,000,000 pounds, but that our butter is selling in Canada at prices such as were indicated a moment ago and that we cannot sell it in competition with anyone else outside of Canada. There was butter landed in Canada within the last few months-landed, but it did not remain here-from New Zealand and Australia, where they are supposed to get good prices for farm products, at 26 cents a pound, while our farmers in Canada are getting for their butter the prices that have been mentioned. We intend to see that our farmers in Canada get that price for their butter, and in doing so we think we are helping the farmer. The greater production of butter this year is putting more money into the pockets of the farmer, and I think the farmer is entitled to it. We intend to carry that policy through as we have it now, with the increased production of butter and whole milk which is bringing a higher price than
IMr. Gardiner.]
it brought before the war. We want the farmer to sell as much whole milk as he can sell in this country, and at present prices he is getting some return.
I agree with the hon. member for Brant that our farmers have to get some attention and consideration. Their wages and costs generally are higher, and in following the policy we are following we are getting more milk out of the cows in Canada than we ever got before, and the farmer is selling more milk than he ever sold before and at a higher average price than has prevailed for a long time. We intend to try to maintain that position, because we realize that the dairy farmer has to put in longer hours and more labour than some of the rest of us who happen to be farmers.

I am: glad that the
Minister of Agriculture is so optimistic, but he would have to be to hold the position he does. I think no other class of people have stepped up to the war effort better than the dairy farmers of this country; that no other class of farmer has had the difficulties which the dairy farmer has had to face. It takes a lot of labour to run a dairy farm and, as hon. members know, labour is so short that the dairy farmer has been up against it for labour. We have come to the point where a lot of dairy farmers in my riding feel they have almost gone to the limit, that they have carried on about as long as they could. Many of them are up in years and they cannot take the hard work that is involved in dairy farming, nor are they entirely satisfied with the treatment they have received. True, they are getting better prices than they ever did before, but they never got enough money before.
There is one place where I think some correction could be made. We have travelling throughout Ontario, and the same perhaps may be said of other provinces, an army of inspectors. A creamery and dairy plant in my own town has five inspectors calling there constantly. Can anyone tell me why five inspectors should call at one plant? I can readily understand that one inspector might call to inspect the electrical equipment, but why five inspectors should call at one plant is more than I can understand. I do not know but that there is some negligence in having so many inspectors going around to these places; because whether you take a quart of cream out of a can or put one in, the test comes out about the same. It is possible, of course, that some of these inspectors are for the Ontario government, but undoubtedly there

War Appropriation-Agriculture
seems to be overlapping in this inspection work, and I think the amount of money that is spent on it could be very well cut, and the producers might then be better satisfied than they are at present.

We have only five
inspectors for the whole province of Ontario, and I do not think they would all call at the one plant on the one day. No doubt there is a health inspector for the town and a health inspector for the county, and probably the province has an agriculture inspector. But so far as this department is concerned we have only five inspectors for 'the whole province, so that if any criticism is due it is not coming to this department.

I was glad to hear the minister say that he was not going to interfere with farmers in this important industry getting what they can for their produce under present circumstances. I believe we have to find ways and means of encouraging greater production of dairy products and meat products, particularly in view of the shortages we have been experiencing for the last several months.
I wonder if the committee realizes the extent to which agriculture has been discouraged and to a large extent neglected during this war period. I do not want to raise the question of aluminum again, but I would just point out that we have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into industry while we have done virtually nothing to improve the apparatus which our fanners have to use to produce their products. I am of the opinion that if we had early in the war adopted a system to encourage our farmers to use better machinery, and had helped them to finance it as we have helped industry to finance its machinery, we would not now be facing these shortages and agriculture would be in a very much better position. Agriculture is an unorganized industry, an industry with very little united power, whereas in other industries we are dealing wtih powerful organizations. I think of some of these concerns to which we have been paying, through the price level, hundreds of millions of dollars. Yet if we had suggested that the farmers increase their production, their herds, let us say, by fifty per cent, and make additions to their barns to give them fifty per cent more capacity, and purchase milking machinery because of the shortage of labour, and if we had said that we would fix a price level that would enable them to pay back during the course of the war the cost of all these things, and make a profit too, what an uproar there would have been! But that is
exactly what we have been doing for some of these big corporations, including the Aluminum Company of Canada.
On Sunday I had the opportunity of seeing the wonderful work that is being done by technicians and ordinary working men at Arvida. I admired that work, but we and our allies are paying for all that, and when I heard the hon. member for Brant speaking this afternoon and realized how little we have done to encourage agriculture, I could not refrain from making the contrast in my mind, especially when I think of the shortages we face in food and dairy products. I hope everything will be done to encourage the dairy industry and other branches of agriculture to get new machinery and new equipment to increase their production, because it will all be needed in the future. To-day we are on short commons. Probably in the future, when the war ends, the demand for food will be so great that we shall have to continue rationing unless we can increase our production to a very large degree. I think some ways and means should be found of enabling the agricultural producers to equip themselves better, improve their herds, and get some machinery to meet the present labour shortage on the farms; and I hope that this will be given some consideration by the government and by the house.

I do not think that I can let these remarks go by without saying something further. I will be the first to admit that, as was stated, I believe by the hon. member for Huron North, farmers are not getting enough, and probably never did get as much as they should get; and I would also be the last to suggest that farmers are getting as much for their products out of the war as some others are. Probably there is a reason for both those conditions which we do not need to discuss to-day. But when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar makes the general statement that hundreds of millions of dollars are going into plants like the Arvida plant as a result of the activities of the government, I think I can also say that hundreds of millions of dollars are going into the pockets of the farming industry to-day, as a result of the activities of the government, though probably not as many hundreds of millions of dollars.
A much larger number of people are involved.

Well, I do not know how many are involved.
An hon. MEMBER; I do.

War Appropriation-Agriculture
My hon. friend says "I do." But when one speaks of all the industries in Canada-
And all their employees.

I am not thinking of
the employees.

-and all the industry of the united nations, I am doubtful, if all those millions cover the cost of getting the materials turned out by plants, as to which of us is dealing with the more people. There is some doubt about that. In any event I do not think I can let the statement go by that the government has been arranging for hundreds of millions of dollars to go into industry, because of the necessity of getting munitions, machines of war, and ships, and that very little or no attention has been paid to agriculture.
One would have to recall that, in the first place, ever since this war began, and before it began, the government has been prepared to take every bushel of wheat which has been delivered to the elevators from western Canada, whether it could be sold or not. Anyone may say that the price is not high enough. I venture to say some of the people in some of the industrial plants will say that the price for their products is not high enough either. But that does not do away with the fact that if the government had not done that, the price would have been a lot lower. We have been taking the wheat and guaranteeing for some time advances of ninety cents a bushel. Before that we were taking wheat at a guaranteed advance of seventy cents.
The minister means, the quota.

No, we were prepared to take every bushel delivered to the elevators with that advance, and sell it to the best advantage we could for the farmer, and eventually give him the benefit of anything we got in addition. Until the last two years this applied to all the wheat. In the last two years it has applied on a quota, but we expect eventually to take it all. We were prepared to do it, and we have been doing it, but the fact is that it has taken hundreds of millions of dollars out of the treasury of Canada to do that job. Whether it is getting enough into the pockets of the farmers is another question, but in answer to the statement that we are providing hundreds of millions of dollars to get munitions and other supplies, is the fact that we are making this provision for the farmer. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that there would not have been an advance from ten- cents a
pound to over twenty cents a pound on cheese if the government had not been prepared ever since the war started to take delivery of every surplus pound of cheese and see that it was properly handled and delivered to Britain. Probably I can say the same thing with regard to pork products.
I know my friends can say, "If you had left the American boundary open you could have sent it all over there at even a higher price." Well, gentlemen in this house who were talking about rationing and about shortages know what that would have meant. Of course in war time, with the great country to the south not in the war until the winter of 1941, and with this country in the war, our products could have gone to the United States, and what would we have been doing in this country? With a nation of 130,000,000 living alongside of us who were in the war, and with their production up very high because of the demands which were made upon them for supplies, and with prices rising there, all the farm products of this country would have gone to the United States, and we would not only have been attempting to produce, as we are to-day, to supply Britain and other countries, but we would have been in other difficulties in addition to those we are in now. In order to safeguard against that, the government, right from the beginning, when we were paying from three to five cents a pound more for hogs than was paid in the United States, took all the hogs in spite of the fact that we could not deliver them all in the first year to Great Britain. In the second year of the war we took them, and we continued to do so all that year, before the United States price began to interfere with the shipment of hogs from this country to Great Britain. Then when it did, we began to pay the United States price and kept our prices up to theirs until the fall of the year, and in the fall of that year a price ceiling was established, which has taken care of the situation from that time. We went to Britain and made an agreement with her, and when the price was higher than she thought she should pay, we added 15 shillings last year to the then price, and this year we added 25 shillings, and for the future we are proposing to pay even a larger proportion than that. To leave out of consideration altogether, w'hat the government has done to help the farmer, is not, I think, being altogether fair in discussing the situation as it exists. Again I come back to the position that anyone can get up and say, "Yes, you first closed the United States boundary." In war time, boundaries are closed everywhere. There is a gentleman in the senate who meets me in the hall once in a while and says, "There are only

TFar Appropriation-Agriculture
two of us left." The first time he said that I asked him, "What do you mean?" He said, "Only two free traders."
Make it three.

I can say this: if we
had our way we would be free traders.
I was going to ask, who was tlie other besides the senator?
He was including me in that.
And me.

But in war time there
is no such thing as free trade. When Britain drew her navy across the oceans she said, "In self-preservation we must see that goods are not carried into Europe. There cannot be any free trade." When Hitler sent his armies out he said, "Not only can there be no free trade, but I am going to take all I want." There cannot be any free trade in the world while that condition prevails. So that we in this country, with our small population as compared with the large populations elsewhere, had to safeguard our position. But even before we had to do that, we paid our own farmers more for some products than they could have obtained even in the United States; and I say to my hon. friends that if they will do what I have done-I have the figures on my desk here, as a matter of fact- and will take the prices as they prevail in the United States and all the costs of getting our products into the United States, it will surprise them to see how close our prices are to those of our neighbours to the south, taking these matters into consideration.
For example, wheat at Winnipeg is from SI to $1.02 a bushel. There is a 42 cent duty on it going into the United States, and if you add that amount to the Winnipeg price you will find that it is not very far from the United States price any day that the market operates. If one considers also freight and exchange, it will be found that in respect of all our products we are very much closer to the United States returns, when our production subsidies are added on top of our price, than most hon. members seem to think we are.
Under these circumstances I just want to emphasize that the government has not forgotten the farmer. We have been doing, I think, as much for the farmer-and I have been in some of the other countries-as most of the nations with which we are allied, and very much more than those against whom we are fighting.

In my opinion these
cows which are going into the United States
should be purchased by the dominion government and distributed in Canada. Whatever device is necessary in order to do that, the government should adopt. You will see a time when we shall be short of dairy products in this country; then it will be too bad, and too late.
I believe that the price we are paying for milk and dairy products generally is too low. We can make all the fine beautiful theories and apologies we desire to make-Liberals are quite strong on that-but the simple fact remains that the price is not high enough at the present time to justify young men going into the farming business and building themselves up. A good deal remains to be done. When the appropriate time comes I intend to discuss the matter of wool. I will not discuss it now.

That will come under
special products.
When the government says that it is being fair to the farmers of this country the government is just completely wrong.

I want to make a brief
plea for Saskatchewan. I should like to see the dairy products board pay a little more attention to that province by assisting them in the matter of producing dairy products. This afternoon's discussion has covered quite a wide field; just recently it extended to the grain business.
Mr. MaoNICOL: And free trade.

We have also had a little
display of competition between the provinces. We heard from British Columbia, and the Ontario members have come to the rescue of their province with respect to the cost of production, particularly of dairy products.
The minister gave some interesting figures with respect to the number of cows in Canada and the price of butter and fluid milk. Also he pointed out that in the production of dairy products long hours and a good deal of labour are required. He made an interesting statement with regard to the number of cows in Canada. Perhaps he will give us the number of dairy cows in Saskatchewan. The statement is interesting when we recall that in 1936 he passed an order whereby the dairy farmers in Saskatchewan had to dispose of their cows, retaining not more than four apart from actual dairy herds. Hon. members will recall that there was a good deal of criticism of that action, because it dealt a severe blow to the dairy industry in that province, and it took the farmers there a little while to get back to the number of cows they had prior to

War Appropriation-Agriculture
that order. It had to do with the necessary relief to farmers in connection with feed and other considerations in that province. I wish the minister would give us a little more information along that line.
With reference to certain remarks made by hon. members representing constituencies in British Columbia and Ontario, I have here a table showing the number of man-power hours required to produce various articles of food that are produced on the farms-butter, cheese, pork, beef, milk and so on-in comparison with similar production in other provinces. Here I want to put in a word for Saskatchewan, because I said that I hoped the dairy board would give some attention to that province. This table shows that it requires, to produce sufficient fluid milk to provide for the needs of one person for a year, 120 manpower hours, which is less than the number required in any other province. I have similar tables for other products, wheat, pork, beef, cheese, butter and so on. Saskatchewan shows up pretty well, and is becoming a diversified farming province. I simply wanted to make this statement to show that Saskatchewan holds a favourable position in regard to the number of man-power hours required to produce a sufficiency of food for one person for a year in any line produced on the farms.
Who made that compilation?
I prepared the table myself.
Oh, oh.

You need not laugh. In my office I have a table which I have taken from the records of the bureau of statistics in Canada and the national research council in the United States. I put the two together and I can produce a comparative table if 'hon. members would like to have it on the record.
The Minister of Agriculture said that the government had paid hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies to Canadian agriculture since the war started.
Do not put words into my mouth. I did not say subsidies. I said that the government provided hundreds of millions to take care of certain farm products, just as it does with regard to other products.
Most of it you got back.

That is true in everything. I noticed that a speech which was made outside the house contained the statement that fifteen per cent of the profit did not come back. If eighty-five per cent of the profit went back, and much of the capital, that is a different matter from representing that every dollar paid remains with the industry.
There has not been that amount of money spent to date in agriculture in Canada, in the way of subsidies, during war time. As a matter of fact, I do not think there has been $100,000,000.
In acreage payment and subsidies there has been much more than $100,000,000 over the period, or pretty close to $100,000,000 in one year.
One hundred million in acreage bonuses and subsidies?
Yes.
Would the minister put the figures on the record to show what has actually been paid?
I will when we get into the wheat acreage reduction under my other estimates. I will give all the figures.
The minister also said that he was one of the few free traders left in the house. How does he explain the government's policy-
I did not say that either. I said that another gentleman so designated me when we met in the hall.

The minister has a nice way of taking credit to himself for what others say. How does he explain the policy , by which the government the other day took the war exchange tax off vegetables coming into the country but did not take it off implements which the producers in Canada require to produce these commodities?

If you look at your
potato speech you will know why.

To be fair, they should at least have taken the 10 per cent war exchange tax off the implements of production that farmers need in order to produce goods of the kind which the government are allowing to come into the country. Since the war started the farmers have been paying approximately 28i per cent in exchange and tariff on the regular line of implements they use, and on some implements as high as 46J per cent. In view of these facts I do not know how the minister can say that he as a member of the present government believes in free trade.

speechtext:
Perhaps I may be
allowed to intervene here. I rather think it would be the feeling of the committee that hon. members should keep within the limits of the item under discussion. The present discussion seems to me to be irrelevant to the item, which has to do with dairy products.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

Occasionally the minister and his supporters take credit for all the money that has been spent to assist agriculture, but I suggest that if we had the figures since the beginning of the war it would be found that they do not amount to over 8 per cent of what industry has received. I will not labour that point. There seems to be a controversy as to who comes from the best dairy province. I come from Manitoba, a province which for seventeen successive years carried off prizes for the best creamery butter produced in that period. As regards the question of creamery inspectors, I am not clear whether this is entirely within provincial jurisdiction or whether there is some liaison between the province and the federal Department of Agriculture. At certain seasons of the year these inspectors are rather lax. Whose responsibility is that?
Cream inspection is all provincial. We have butter graders and people who inspect products going out of the province, but the inspection of cream is all done by provincial men.

I will try to keep within the confines of the item, but seeing that there has been some latitude in the discussion I should like to place on the record certain facts I have discovered in a return that was tabled on June 16 by the Department of Finance in response to a motion of the hon. member for Megantic-Frontenac (Mr. Lafontaine). The return shows the numbers and the amounts of repayments made by farmers in each province who obtained loans from the Canadian farm loan board during the years from 1938 to 1942 inclusive. After all, perhaps the measuring stick of prosperity of agriculture may be determined to a large extent by the ability of the farmers to retire their indebtedness. I would point out that possibly the provinces that produced dairy products have enjoyed a little greater prosperity through the difficult times than other provinces that do not produce these commodities. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made a plea for the farmer, he will probably be interested in an analysis which I have made of that return. I should like the hon. member for Huron North also to follow closely the observations I shall make as a result of some Ripleyizing I have done of the return in question. It gives the number of payments made by the farmers in the various provinces in the years indicated and the amount of money that has been paid out, and I have averaged it and discovered that in Ontario, for every dollar paid on the farm loan in 1938, the farmer had been able to pay $1.73 in 1943.
At the expense of the rest of Canada.

That was to the end of March. No, it is not at the expense of the rest of Canada. I am speaking of the ability of farmers to retire their indebtedness, and Ontario has made the best record in spite of the fact that we are not supposed to be farmers in that province.
That record is attributable to the fact that you have an industrial market at your door.

That may have some bearing on it, but in answer to the hon. member for Souris I suggest that we analyse the figures for Manitoba. Manitoba is not as far from industrial markets as Saskatchewan. For every dollar his province paid in 1938, only 69 cents was paid in 1943. And there is Saskatchewan.
The boys are all in the army in Manitoba.
They were not in 1938. Then it goes on-
Are those payments made with respect to dairy produce?
No; these are total payments made to the federal farm loan organization upon mortgages. These are repayments on the loan.
What has that to do with this item?

I am carrying out the argument offered by the Minister of Agriculture that the contribution this government has made to agriculture, by way of subsidies and encouragement to agriculture, has been substantial, and that we are getting results, as indicated by the ability of farmers m the various provinces to retire their indebtedness. Is there any other better measuring stick to substantiate the argument offered by the minister than the ability of farmers to .pay off the mortgages? I think that is one of the best measuring sticks possible.
The hon. member should take that up with the Minister of Finance. Let the Minister of Agriculture get his statement there.

The hon. member for Souris is one hon. member who is most talkative about getting some advantage for the farmer. I say you cannot divorce financing from farming, when measuring the prosperity of agriculture.
War Appropriation-Agriculture
I do not see any hope of getting any help from the hon. member's speech.

I insist upon, placing this
record on Hansard, for the benefit of the hon. member for Souris.
Mr. Chairman, are we discussing farm indebtedness or dairy production? I understand a bill will be introduced later, and that it will deal with the matter of farm indebtedness.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the point is well taken. I must confess I have allowed considerable latitude, but I think the time has arrived when we should confine ourselves to the item.
Mr. Chairman, are you going to allow the discussion to continue?

I shall try to comply with the ruling, and I shall complete my observations as soon as possible. What I have said is, I believe, the conclusion which must be drawn in connection with the matter of the prosperity of the farmers in Canada.
What is the hon. member's figure for Saskatchewan?

I am glad the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is interested. In spite of the difficulty that province has had with the drouth condition it has a creditable record. For every dollar paid on farm loan in 1938, they have paid S1.08 in 1943. On top of that, four times as many loans are being paid in 1943 as in 1938.
But let us not forget that 1938 followed the worst year we ever had.

I agree with that. That condition was reflected over a period of years. For every dollar Alberta paid in 1938 they have paid only 84 cents in 1943.
In conclusion, there seems to be something -and I do not know whether it is coincidental or not-which might be said with respect to Alberta and Manitoba. I have noticed that they are the only two provinces which have not been able to measure up, in the repayment of their mortgages, with the other provinces. It will be noticed that they are the only two provinces unfortunate enough not to have an honest-to-goodness Liberal government. Perhaps that has had something to do with their position.
Did the hon. member use the word "fortunate"?
I said that those two provinces were unfortunate enough not to have Liberal governments, and that their condition may be on account of that fact.
My hon. friend has a good sense of humour, and I am sure when he made that statement he was exercising it.
The Prime Minister will maintain, probably, that they should not have five cents' worth of assistance.

I have been interrupted considerably in placing this analysis before the committee. This is a most interesting return, so far as the position of agriculture is concerned. The only thing I can say is that the leader of the hon. member for Souris, who is nowr running at large, had the administration of that province for about twenty years, and yet they do not seem to have had the same degree of prosperity as farmers in some other parts of Canada.
Manitoba has had the best administration in Canada in the last few years.

The Minister of Agriculture is probably aware that for a considerable length of time in northwest Saskatchewan our farmers have been getting together to discuss ' those various matters which would permit their going ahead and making the greatest possible contribution to the war effort. In the last year, over a hundred farm production gatherings were held in that area. As a result of the discussions we have found out some interesting facts. Roughly speaking, we have in the area of North Battleford about 10,000 farmers. Those people agree that if they could have only one more milch cow on each farm they would be able to produce 2,000,000 more pounds of butter each year. That indicates what can be done on a small scale, by many farmers who are not big producers. They have had very little assistance.
These discussions have brought out the fact that the majority of our farming people are unable to expand, and for two reasons. First of all, those who have fair-sized herds are afraid to increase because they lack a guarantee as to future price. Then, the smaller farmers have not derived any great benefit from the bonuses. They may have only fifteen or twenty acres decrease from wheat, and therefore the amount they would get from the bonus would be very small. They still have a little wheat, which they are unable to sell. Many of those farmers have one or two young cattle or young

War Appropriation-Agriculture
heifers. However, week after week they are being forced to sell their cattle before they are finished. We have estimated that if each farmer could keep the cattle he has, we could produce ab'out 20,000,000 more pounds of beef from that area alone.
I know our farmers are supporting the provincial government's scheme with respect to farm committees. I was wondering, however, if the Minister of Agriculture would tell us whether it would be possible to initiate a scheme whereby some assistance could be given to the smaller farmers to allow them to keep their stock, if they lack at the present time that little bit of cash necessary to carry on farm production. If this assistance were given, instead of having to slaughter their young cattle our farmers would be encouraged to keep them. Then, has the question of future prices been discussed by the government?
Has the quota of milking machines been raised in 1943 over the 1942 figure?

I understand the quota has been raised, but I am not in a position to say by how much. There is provision made for milking machines, and a further provision for obtaining transformers to step down electrical power, so that farmers can have more opportunity to operate milking machines. Both these things have been done to the greatest possible extent.

Item agreed to.
Special products board - administration, $49,459.

Unfortunately I
could not be here last night because I had to meet a train. But it is clear that we have teamwork in British Columbia, because the hon. member for New Westminster spoke for me. Some statements were made in connection with the dehydration of potatoes which were not strictly in accordance with the facts. I should like to have the record straight in that connection.
Among other statements was one that for some reason or another we cannot get an order for our plant in British Columbia. At this point I should like to know if that plant is not bona fides, or if the owner is not bona fides. We should like to be told that and we think we are entitled to be told that. This plant was passed by one of the officials. It was passed by Mr. Atkinson, an employee of the federal Department of Agriculture, a man who is employed for that very purpose. Then, we are told the plant is not capable
of handling this job. In fact, we were told last night that we could not produce in the Fraser valley and in the constituency of New Westminster potatoes equal to those found in other parts of the world. Well, I am not going to boast; I am going to tell the straight facts.
