The constituencies of both Fraser Valley and New Westminster produce potatoes better than any others on the north American continent.
We have been told that the plant in British Columbia cannot get a contract. Two excuses have been given to us. We are told that it must be capable of producing, and that it must pass the requirements. We admit it is only right that it should meet those requirements. I repeat that the plant has been inspected by Mr. Atkinson, and that it has been passed by him. The second excuse is that we must guarantee that we shall not be a deficiency area. May I point out that neither the experts in the federal Department of Agriculture, nor those in any other department, can tell whether or not we shall have a deficiency area. Just this afternoon the .minister said that owing to exceptional weather we shall have one of the heaviest hay crops ever known in Ontario. I wonder how much hay could have been harvested yesterday or the day before, in that kind of weather. What a ridiculous statement to make-that they could guarantee that there would be a surplus crop! I repeat that no department in any part or province of Canada can guarantee that we shall have a surplus in any crop such as potatoes.
I do not believe I could bring a better witness as to the truth of that statement than the Minister of Agriculture himself, one of the most competent men in agriculture on the north American continent. I do not know what better evidence I can produce to prove that the officials of his own department do not know what they are talking about when they say that they can definitely state whether or not we shall have sufficient potatoes. I quote this from Hansard at page 4372.
Mr. Gardiner: There is considerable difficulty in determining very long in advance whether there will be a shortage.
A little lower down on the page, referring to victory gardens, he is reported to have said:
If they have been responding to the appeals we have been making, it is very difficult for anyone to estimate how many potatoes we shall have this fall.
That is the Minister of Agriculture speaking, who also tells us that the only reason this plant cannot get an order to handle surplus potatoes is that we cannot guarantee that we shall have a surplus.

I gave three reasons.
War Appropriation-Agriculture
I should like to put this letter on the record. It is under date of Ottawa, June 7, and two paragraphs read as follows-
I gave three reasons last night.

This was sent to me after I had been trying month after month to get a plant in British Columbia to handle our surplus potatoes. I quote:
1.	That the plant is properly and completely equipped with the necessary machinery for preprocessing and dehydrating in order to do the job;
2.	That the agricultural supplies board could be assured by competent provincial authority that the dehydration of whatever quantity of potatoes might be decided upon in the Fraser valley will not in any way short the domestic market in the coast area, a point in which the foods administration of the wartime prices and trade board is vitally interested.
That is signed by the Minister of Agriculture. Those are the principal reasons we cannot get it. Is it the desire of the government to create little Balkan states within Canada? Last year one organization produced some 14,153-25 tons of potatoes, and Mr. Langdon, the district horticulturist, estimates that we shall have from thirteen to fifteeen thousand tons more this year. Then the authority on potatoes and other farm crops, Mr. Donald Gordon, comes out to British Columbia and is reported to have said, among other things, that the farmer would produce whether it pays or not. At a time when there was no shortage of potatoes this wartime prices and trade board, which was not advised by any practical agriculturist, placed a ceiling on the different grades of potatoes. Prices were set at a point which will ruin this organization which is owned and controlled by the farmers and which was originally set up by the federal and provincial governments to be operated under the provincial department of agriculture. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to note that at no time did this organization refuse to market potatoes to the armed forces or to anyone else. At no time did they advise their producers not to do that. But this price board cut the ceiling price some thirteen dollars and expected us to go on selling. Then they said we were a deficiency area, that we could not produce the potatoes. This at a time when hundreds of tons of potatoes were rotting annually. The minister said last night that he was not interested-I do not mean that he wanted to see food wasted-in so far as dehydration was concerned in what had been lost last year or a few years ago. Here is what was advised by the experts 
we have over here. The minister is reported at page 4369 of Hansard as follows:

not five years ago or six years ago, or even last year-but that there would be sufficient potatoes this year to warrant the board's going in there and buying potatoes to be dehydrated for shipment out, when there may have to be potatoes shipped in to feed the people in that area.
How many hundreds of tons of potatoes have been shipped into Ontario this year, and yet there are two plants in Ontario? According to the evidence given in the agriculture committee, they brought in potatoes and yet have given contracts for 250 tons of potatoes from New Brunswick to be dehydrated. Here is something else that interests me, and I think the people of British Columbia will also be interested. The minister is reported at page 4369 of Hansard as follows:
If that can be proved satisfactorily, then there is no reason why a contract should not be given. That matter, I believe, has been referred to the wartime prices and trade board-
The wartime prices and trade board were to say whether we can produce enough potatoes in British Columbia or anywhere else; the wartime prices and trade board which is to tell us everything about agriculture. I continue:
-and I presume they had evidence before making the statement-that while it is true that British Columbia has been exporting potatoes, that very much larger quantities are imported from points outside the province. Considerable quantities move from interior points, such as Ashcroft and Kamloops. The wartime prices and trade board state it is their opinion that a dehydration programme at the coast would accentuate this movement which, under wartime conditions, would not appear to be justified.
Kamloops and Ashcroft are not in my district, but I do not think there is any district on the north American continent, and I say this with due deference to the 'maritimes, which is more famous for its potatoes. I am sure that the minister's officials might know that. These points are only 150 to 200 miles from Vancouver, and yet it is proposed to set up little Balkan states so that potatoes cannot move into Vancouver or Victoria. I quote again:
That is their decision on the information they have, up to the moment. They point out that there are so many potatoes being used there that there is some question as to whether we should dehydrate potatoes in British Columbia.
That is the decision of the board whose head has said "that farmers will produce whether they make any money or not," Unfortunately that is true because the farmer has been foolish enough in the past to do just that. We are told that we must not

War Appropriation-Agriculture
send potatoes from Ashcroft or Kamloops to Vancouver if we want a contract to dehydrate our surplus potatoes which have been rotting on the ground. I wonder if the wartime prices and trade board, which apparently has had so much to do with this matter that it has been afraid to appear before the agriculture committee, will give a guarantee to the farmers and the people of Canada that surplus potatoes will not rot in these days of want if we do not get this order.
I hold no brief for this particular company. To the best of my knowledge the owner is a prominent political opponent of mine; but I do object to discrimination being shown, not only to this plant but to the farmers in my province and in my riding, in refusing an order for dehydration on two grounds. The first was that the plant must be up to standard. I am willing to accept that, but it has been passed, so we are informed by their own engineers and we have the report. The second point is that somebody is to say whether we shall have a lot of rain. When you go out ten miles from Ottawa, as I did last Sunday, you can see potatoes with four inches of water over them. Can anyone tell whether you will have a surplus? I want a more definite reason from the minister.
I disagree entirely with him that the Fraser valley and New Westminster are deficiency areas. I disagree with him, or with his officials, when it is said that our potatoes are not up to quality. I think the people of British Columbia are entitled to know why a contract to dehydrate potatoes or other vegetables has not been given. It is obvious that the department has no fear that we are not going to have potatoes, but it is anxious to repeat its actions of past years, as was referred to by the hon. member for New Westminster, and permit southern potatoes to come in just when ours are beginning to come on the market. Not only that, but the department adds insult to injury by reducing the price of potatoes, as it did last week, when our own are just coming on the market. The ceiling price of new potatoes is restricted to that of old potatoes. Is there a farmer, even in Ontario, where apparently they are satisfied with farm prices, who will tell you that you can produce new potatoes in June at the cost of old potatoes? I am sorry I was not here last night. I was in the chamber most of the day and heard a lot of nonsense, and then I had to go and do some business. I should like the minister to tell me why this plant cannot be given a contract. Is it because the plant is not satisfactory? Is the man who owns it not reliable? Incidentally it is the
only dehydrating plant in the Dominion of Canada that has not had one dollar toward the purchase of machinery or anything else.

All I can do is to give the same answer I gave last night. I notice the hon. member for New Westminster is not in the chamber, but I should like to apologize to him for having said last night that I did not use the word "vegetables". When I read Hansard I found I had used it once.
The hon. member spoke on my behalf, so that I will accept the apology on his behalf.

I am one who perhaps is not enough of a botanist to be able to distinguish between vegetables and potatoes. The answer which I gave last night covered three points. What I said was that if the Haney plant can be fully and properly equipped for the dehydration of potatoes and manufacture a product which will meet the board's specifications, and if the wartime prices and trade board will approve the production of additional dehydrated potatoes in British Columbia, the special products board could give any plant a contract for a small quantity of dehydrated potatoes in 1943, possibly 200 tons.
The reason why we state a small quantity is that the plants which are operating are producing all that we have required up to the moment. This question has been under discussion for some time, and I think I explained to the hon. member for Fraser Valley before this discussion even started in this house that we were considering giving this plant a contract for a limited amount, provisional upon their having the necessary equipment to produce the product, and provisional, too, upon the prices board agreeing to the contract being given. It is true that the decision would depend upon whether they are satisfied that there are sufficient potatoes in the Fraser valley to take care of the demands in the valley, but I doubt whether anyone has used the argument that anyone has been able to determine up to date whether that would be the case or not. I venture to say that even plants which are now producing dehydrated potatoes, if they could get more for their fresh potatoes, would not bother to dehydrate them. I gave one other reason last night, namely, that we were getting potatoes at thirty-three cents a pound in Alberta, at thirty-two cents at other points, and that British Columbia was suggesting thirty-five * cents. Of course we were hoping that we could get the product at the same price as
War Appropriation-Agriculture

elsewhere but that was not a condition in the statement I have made. The statement is that if they can produce a plant properly equipped and if we can get the consent of the wartime prices and trade board, which would be dependent on whether there are sufficient potatoes to take care of the demands in the valley, there will be no doubt about a contract being given for the limited amount stated here. I cannot see that we can do any more than that.

I thank the minister. I am not quarrelling with his department or with the assistance we have been given in the past and are receiving to-day and will no doubt receive in the future, but the only approach to the prices board that a member has who represents a farming district is through the minister. I might just as well bump my head against the Queen Victoria monument out here as talk to the prices board. In the first place, in my opinion they do not know anything about *whether or not there will be enough potatoes. As to price, the order of the prices board last year gave Alberta and British Columbia interior farmers a higher ceiling price by S4 a ton on Canada No. 1 potatoes and $8 a ton on Canada No. 2 potatoes in the Vancouver market than that received by coast growers for the same grades. Yet it is suggested that we must receive thirty-two cents or lower. As I have said, I have no other approach to the wartime prices and trade board nor has any other private member of this house than through the minister.

I should have said that we have already written to the owners of the plant asking if they can give us information on which we can base a decision on the question of equipment. We are hoping for a reply from them and will then communicate with the hon. member.
I accept that, because when the minister undertakes to do anything he completes it, but I cannot say that for the wartime prices and trade board.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that we can discuss wool on this item. I would ask the minister to tell us why the price of wool is at its present figure. I expect to be told immediately that provision has been made for a four cent increase in the price by way of subsidy, provided the wool is put into a certain condition, and provided that the province will pay one-half of the subsidy. Wool was one of the first commodities to be brought under control at the outbreak of war, and so far as I know the price of wool is the same now as it was before the war. I do not think

that is fair to the wool growers. They seem to be unable to help themselves, and I would suggest that the government, either the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Finance, under which the wartime prices and trade board comes, do something to increase the price of wool at the present time.
I am wondering if the minister really wants wool production in Canada increased.

A year ago we embarked on the definite policy of trying to increase the sheep population in Canada in order to increase our wool production. We have had some success in that, although I have not the figures with me at the moment as to the extent to wffiich the sheep population has been increased. But it has increased, and we are still carrying out that policy. Hon. members know that the day war was declared, even before that, Britain had secured the whole wool supply of all parts of the empire, and Canada along with other parts of the empire came into that arrangement. We had an undertaking to take our deliveries from that set-up, the same as all other peoples who were cooperating with Britain in the war. That condition still exists. We made that undertaking with Britain in the first year of the war when it was not possible otherwise, to get wool to make uniforms for the troops or for any other purpose. This is now the fourth year of the war, and that arrangement still exists. The position at the beginning of this year was that we had all the .wool in Canada we needed, whether or not we got an increase in our own production; that is, we had all the wool we needed if we carried out that agreement. We cannot hope to produce anything like what we require ; we have to depend on the pool for part of our requirements, but we do not require to get any more wool for our purposes in Canada beyond the deliveries under the agreement. In spite of that, we did go ahead to subsidize the production of wool if the provinces would pay half the cost of the subsidy. I think nearly all the provinces are paying half the subsidy now; I am certain Alberta pays.
Coming back to the question whether we could do better if we sold our wool elsewhere, the last time I looked up the figures, which was only a few weeks ago, they showed that we could not obtain, as much by shipping to the United States as we could obtain in our own market. The United States is the only other market available, and our farmers are getting a better return by selling in their own market.

War Appropriation-Agriculture
How is that?

In the first place, there is a duty on wool going into the United States, and other costs in getting the wool there. Those who figured out the position figured out a comparative price for me because I was interested in finding out just what the position of the Canadian farmer is as compared with the farmer in the United States, and the position of the Canadian farmer in comparison with what his position would be if he shipped to the United States market. I found that as. far as wool is concerned our farmers are in a better position than they would be in if the wool were being marketed in the United States when all the costs of getting it there are taken into account. Those are the facts, and I would suggest that we are doing fairly well. We do not think we are doing all that the sheep people might expect or all that they might be entitled to, but we are doing all that we have thought it was advisable to do under existing circumstances.

The minister says that we are doing as well now as if we had access to the United States market, but what I am trying to find out is what the Canadian farmer could ge't in dollars and cents as compared with the United States farmer. According to the press, the farmer in Montana has been receiving from 37J to 55 cents a pound for "wool, which is a much higher price than we are getting here, and in addition the United States dollar will buy much more than our Canadian dollar. So that there is really no comparison between the prices obtained by the farmer in Canada and those obtained by the farmer in the United States.

I had forgotten to mention one point. The price is very much higher now than it whs before the war. The price before the war w-as, I think, about 16 cents; it is now around 30 cents, with a subsidy of 4 cents. The price in the United States for the same grade of wmol is about 54i cents; but when one takes all the charges and the duty and everything else into consideration, the return to the Canadian farmer, with the subsidy, is slightly better than the return he would have if he sold his wool in the United States.
What is the United States duty on wool?
I have forgotten what it is, but it was all figured in the price.

I was trying to get at the number of cents a pound received by the farmer here
and by the farmer in the United States. If I remember correctly, the price of wool last year was 30 cents a pound. At the present time, with the extra 4 cents, it will be 34 cents a pound. The price in the United States is much higher. The fact that our price is 34 cents a pound this year compared with 16 cents before the war will not convince us that two wrongs can make a right, because before the war the price of wool, as of several other farm products, was far below the cost of production or what it should have been.

I am not going to try to put my figuring against my hon. friend's figures. I got the best statistician in the department to figure for me, and he came back with the statement that one could not get as much here for the same quality of wool in the United States as is being paid, in the conditions prevailing here, by shipping it to the markets there. The market here gives a better return. I have the figures in my office, I do not happen to have them on my desk, but I can produce them.

My point is that I should like to have the market price in Canada raised to the price in the United States market, because it is only after taking into consideration the freight charges and the duty that the comparison which the minister makes can be made.
What is the date of the order in council passed in the spring, under which a bonus was to be given to the farmers?
It is a quality bonus; it is paid on only a certain quality of wool.
It was passed on March 29, was it not?
About then. It was around that time.

Does the minister contend that, when an order in council is passed on the 29th of March to give farmers a bonus for high quality wool, particularly clean wool, he is giving the farmer anything like a chance to prepare clean wool?

I would say in reply
to that that I was probably affected a little at the time the date was set, by some criticisms which were made in this house previously. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made an announcement on the floor of the house with regard to wheat, and a number of hon. members rose and criticized him for having made it alleging that the farmers had not a chance to present their representations. A farm delegation notified me that they were
War Appropriation-Agriculture

coming here about wool, and I waited before we made the decision and put the order in council through until I heard what they had to say. They came here at that time of the year and asked for it, and I presume it was of some benefit to them or they would not have asked for it.

Certainly it was not
giving the farmers any chance at all to qualify for the bonus. That is perfectly clear. I wonder if the committee could know when Doctor Barton's letter was sent out to the various provinces telling them of this new arrangement?

Right after that, but
whether the letter got there or not, it was announced in this house right at the time, and I think it was pretty well known.

In other words, the
provinces would not get word until along in April, would they?
It would be in April.

Which made it completely impossible for the people who had not been particularly preparing that clean wool to qualify for the bonus. In other words, the bonus was offered and taken away at the same time.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the purchase of butter in order to maintain the price established by the wartime prices and .trade board and to pay necessary storage, insurance and freight charges thereon, $1,500,000.

Would the minister make
a statement on the amount of butter that has been purchased by the board, the dates of the purchases, and the import position in Canada with regard to butter last year and this year?

I would have to speak
from memory in giving a figure, but the amount of butter which was purchased was somewhere between three and four million pounds. The amount represented by this item would indicate about what was necessary in order to carry through the transaction.
The position is this, that when butter goes down to a certain price we undertake to purchase it. There was about a week, between the going out of the old season and the coming in of the new, when we found ourselves obligated to take butter off the market because the price had dropped below the floor. We took the butter off the market and we still have it.

How much butter is on hand in Canada, and how does the amount compare with other years? I believe the general feeling in my community is that the butter situation is a very difficult one for the farmers. All the evidence I have is that there are large stocks of butter on hand in spite of rationing, and the farmer who makes his own butter is breaking the law if he makes more than the limit the law allows him. I have had many constituents come in to see me claiming that though they have butter on hand they cannot sell it; they have made it but there is no market for it; they are not supposed to have it. There is a danger of farmers running short of butter who could make it for themselves and their neighbours. I submit that, if there is anything like the required amount of butter in storage, and the consumer could use more, it is a great detriment to the farmer to ration butter, because it prohibits the farmer from selling his own products. I feel that if many of us in this chamber were prohibited from carrying on our own businesses the way in which the farmer is prevented from making his livelihood in his own way and selling his own products, we should look at this question in a vastly different way from the way many of us do.

The amount in storage in July was 26,000,000 pounds; one year ago it was 14,000,000 pounds; so that there are now 12,000,000 pounds more butter in storage than there was on the first of July a year ago.
"With regard to the other question, as I stated a few moments ago, the floor price at the beginning of this year was thirty-two cents. It goes up three-eighths of a cent each month, and is now 32% cents. The government is obligated to buy all butter when the price goes down to the floor. We have not bought any since the beginning of this dairy year, which indicates that the price has never been down to the floor. So that although it is said that the farmer has not been able to sell, the fact is that he has been able to sell all his butter at a price higher than the floor, and then he gets the subsidy on top of the price. The price has been around thirty-three cents, always a little above the floor. It is added to by the subsidy of eight cents a pound on butter fat, which has been in force ever since the beginning of the period.
The other question, whether we should stop rationing, is a question of policy, of course, upon which I cannot make any comment at the moment other than to say that we are still rationing.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

Surely the minister appreciates that the rationing restrictions affecting the sale of butter have an all-important bearing on the salability and the price received by the producer. It is much the same as the market for rhubarb around the city [DOT] of Ottawa this year. You could get twenty-five cents a bushel if you could sell it at all, but you could not sell it.

It could not make much difference. They are buying butter for sale next winter. The price is set as it is, going up three-eighths of a cent each month, because that will pay the carrying charges on the butter, and the man who buys in May or June has to have his three-eighths of a cent each month to carry it until January of next year, when he is going to sell it, so that the price of butter could not be much higher if the ceiling price is to be thirty-five cents. He is getting all there is in it if he is to carry it and still have the thirty-five cents. We have taken care of that condition by providing a subsidy of eight cents in the summer and ten cents in the winter, and this puts up the return to the farmer, as against twenty-six cents at which butter was laid down in this country a short time ago.
But the rationing policy means that he cannot even sell on the local market without coupons - which makes it impossible for him to do so.
He gets exactly the same price. He can sell it at that.
But he cannot sell it.
If there is anyone who has been unable to sell his butter at 32% cents, the government will buy it. You can tell him that.

If the minister will tell us how much butter has spoiled in storage, and how many complaints he has received from local warehousemen about the butter they have on hand which they cannot dispose of at an economic price, he will complete the picture, but until he does so his argument will not seem true to me.

The butter broker or merchant has never done anything else at any other time. He cannot carry on business in any other way. We produce most of our butter in the summer months, and we consume in the winter months twice as much as we produce. Anyone engaged in the butter business has to buy his surplus in the summer and carry it until the winter. We take care
of that by raising the price three-eighths of a cent each month. He can buy in May or June ' or July and get his carrying charges under this system. In previous years, it is true, he might buy at twenty cents and sell at thirty-five cents and make an enormous profit. He cannot do that during war time, but he can buy it and get all his costs guaranteed and carry it through to the winter months. Men in the butter business are bound to be storing at present. They do not want to sell it; they are carrying it to the winter months to sell it then at the ceiling and make the cost of storage.

That is exactly the point. That is a benefit to the man who handles butter. It is no asset to the man who produces butter. I realize that it is not the minister's department that makes the regulations, but I took this matter up about a month ago. A farmer in my community manufactured in the spring approximately sixty pounds of butter for the use of his family before sending any of his product to the dairy. After rationing came in, the farmers realized that they were breaking the law by holding so much of their own home-made butter for their own use, and they reported the situation to the ration officer, surrendering their coupons. They asked what they should do with the butter and the answer was to sell it. They tried to sell it, but they could not get the coupons for it, except for one or two pounds, from this man here and there. It was simply impossible for them to sell the butter. They went back to the office and asked what they were to do and the officer there simply threw up his hands and said, "I cannot tell you, but you have to get rid of it." That is the situation, and surely that must have a detrimental effect on the production of butter in the country, especially when we are rationed to the limit, cutting down home consumption of butter materially. The matter is very serious. It is one of the elements that cause trouble and discontent, and it is very hard on our farmers. Perhaps the minister can tell us something about spoiled butter.

There must be a misunderstanding somewhere. I do not know of any regulation that prevents a farmer from producing dairy butter and keeping it in his cellar, and if there were, there is a stabilization corporation which has undertaken to buy from them and pay a price for it. That has been known for months. When the stabilization corporation went out to look for all this dairy butter they could find only 7,000 pounds in all Canada for sale. In other words, I find it difficult to follow the story my hon. friend is telling.
War Appropriation-Agriculture

Nevertheless it is an actual fact. The regulations stipulate that no one may keep on hand more butter than the ration authorities permit, and sixty pounds is more than these people could keep, with the size of their family. It is all very well to say that they can dispose of their dairy butter, but no dealer will buy butter made by a farmer when he can buy creamery butter made by the dairies, and the farmers cannot market the product.

When the rationing of butter was announced last year there was a very wide division of public opinion as to whether it would be a success, or whether it was necessary, in view of the complex nature of the proposal. It was contended that there was no scarcity of butter and therefore no need to ration the commodity. I argued that rationing should be under the control of the Department of Agriculture, under the minister himself, and there was a great deal of discussion in the newspapers, among consumers' leagues, bodies in the retail business and other organizations in the country with regard to the desirability or the necessity or the usefulness of such a proposal in an agricultural country like Canada, which has a vast agriculture dominion organization for this industry, and another one under provincial direction. I contended at the time that it was absolutely useless for us to hand over to the wartime prices and trade board a technical matter of this sort, because many of the people comprising the board have no practical experience either in agriculture or in business, wholesale or retail, or in the production and marketing of butter, and other food commodities. During the past year we have spent S65,000,000 in a subsidy programme, and this programme will be costing this fiscal year from $90,000,000 to 8100,000,000. There was a great deal of blowing about the success of rationing in Canada as compared with the United States, but people seem to forget that in the United States there is a population of well over 100,000,000 people, whereas we have but a small population. Moreover, they have more complex problems than we have, owing to greater population and area and greater variety of trade and production.
I should like to find out from the minister what coordination there is with the control board in the direction of this whole rationing scheme. I repeat, it and also beef rationing, should have been left under the present minister, in the Department of Agriculture. That was the opinion I expressed a year ago and I am still of that opinion. It should have been left to a responsible minister of

the crown. Had that been done matters would have been far different. It would have been far better than leaving it with some college professor who knows no more about butter than what he consumes himself. The policy was all wrong. I should like either the Minister of Agriculture or any other cabinet minister to tell this committee why there should be any scarcity of such an important food commodity as butter, and so much faulty distribution. Rationing of butter has not been a success; at any rate, it has not been the success that it should have been. It has cost us a great deal of money with a huge organization, and there has been a lot of waste and useless duplication. Ration books are issued, and before they are used new books are brought out. I should like to have a statement from the minister. I have looked into this question a great deal, both during the recess of parliament and since, and I suggest to the minister that if he has time, when the house gets through with its business, he should look up the June number of the monthly booklet of the National City Bank of New York city and see what that publication has to say with regard to the effectiveness of subsidies in the United States. Let me quote a few passages from this booklet under the heading, "Subsidies conditioned on economics."
Canadian subsidies are tied directly with regulation of profit margins on the particular product. They are designed to cover only a part of the increase in costs, and are conditioned upon adoption of various economies in production, importation and distribution.
It gives reasons why there should be a limit to rationing many of these commodities. I think the time has come when we should have a statement from the government in connection with the whole matter.

I am interested in the opinions of the hon. member with regard to the last matter he spoke of, but he will realize that it is impossible for me to discuss that point. It is a matter of policy which has been decided, and the prices board is under the Minister of Finance.
On the other question as to this particular arrangement, with regard to the purchase of butter, that is not arranged by the prices board. The Department of Agriculture sets a floor price, and the department protects that floor by purchasing butter when butter goes down to the floor, so that 81,500,000 is provided with which to buy butter when it goes to the floor, to prevent its going further. That is an arrangement which is made entirely in the Department of Agriculture to protect the

War Appropriation-Agriculture
farmer against an unusual drop in butter prices. The extent to which it can drop with the widest margin is 3 cents, but at the present time it is 2} cents, until we have to step in and purchase.
I asked a question with regard to the amounts purchased by this board last year and the dates of purchase.
I gave that figure.
The minister did not give the dates purchased. Did he give figures with regard to imports of butter?

It was the last week before this present year came in, the week beginning May 1. It was in the month of April, and our year in connection with dairy products comes in on May 1. These regulations would apply to May 1.
In reply to the hon. member for Broadview, I may say that this policy was announced prior to the 1st of May, to cover the whole year from May 1, 1943, to May 1, 1944. This money is to carry out that policy.
Where is this butter stored at the present time?
There are nine different cities across Canada in which it is stored. It is in storage right across the country.
What companies?
It would be in cold storage plants in those cities.	M
Not government cold storage plants?
No.

Has the minister any particulars as to the amount of spoiled butter, unfit for human consumption in Canada, and has he further information as to what butter, if any, has been sold for other than consumption purposes?
We have no information as to any spoiled creamery butter in Canada. We have no knowledge of any such thing.
Has the minister figures with regard to imports of butter?
They are very small. There was the butter I referred to a while ago which was landed in Canada but which we are shipping out again, if it is not all shipped now.
The minister has no particulars about the spoilt butter. Has he any information about dairy butter?
None.
There is another question about the subsidy on butter. I understand no subsidy is paid on dairy butter, but there is a subsidy on that delivered to the creameries.
The subsidy is paid on butter fat, not on butter, either creamery or dairy. There is a subsidy paid on any butter fat delivered to the creamery.
There seems to be a good deal of dissension about the subsidy, because there is discrimination against those who are not located close enough to the creamery to deliver butter fat.

I gave an answer a moment ago which was to the effect that we have set up prices by which the government is prepared to abide, for dairy butter, where there is any difficulty about it. But we have not been able to find much of it anywhere in Canada.
Will the government purchase dairy butter from the farmers?
There would be a price paid which the government guarantees.
A price which will not compare with the creamery price.
It will not be as high as the creamery price.
Has the minister any figures as to the percentage of butter now in storage which was imported last year?

The total amount of butter imported in 1942 was 592,000 pounds. That is, of course, just butter which comes across the boundary line at different points, or at least the greater part of it. I cannot tell how much of that is in storage to-day. I imagine it is practically all eaten.
Where was that butter shipped to?
The butter I mentioned earlier was shipped to Halifax.
The minister says that the butter imported was almost all from the United States.
I cannot tell the point to which butter was shipped.
The minister cannot say where it was imported from.
It was received at points all the way along the boundary; it would come over at different points.

Item agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
4402	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Wartime prices and trade board-administration, $14,300,000.

Mr. Chairman, in time
of war it is often, necessary to set up commissions so that the government may share the responsibilities of administration. We are now discussing the administration of one of these commissions, namely, the wartime prices and trade board, which operates under the authority of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I do not intend to delay the committee unduly, but I should like to refer to a special case, the characteristics of which almost constitute a question of privilege in connection with myself. That being so, I feel I am entitled to discuss the matter with the minister. I do not bear any grudge against anyone, either against the minister or any of the parties involved in this case, but I want to clear up my position, as a member of this house and as a public man who, I believe, has had a rather good public and private reputation.
The wartime prices and trade board established in Mont Laurier, the principal town in my riding, an office which is in charge of a representative appointed in the usual way by the civil service commission in cooperation with the wartime prices and trade board officials. This man is Mr. Alphonse Forget. During the summer of 1942 I received many complaints about the handling of tire sale permits. It was alleged that this representative was using the privileges attached to his office to divert all tire sale permits to a certain garage in Mont Laurier. I made a personal investigation, and I thought it was my duty to put the results of this investigation before the proper authorities. This I did at the beginning of December, 1942.
At the end of November the investigator who had been appointed to this office, a Mr. Pellerin, was suddenly dismissed without any apparent reason. While I was in Montreal I received a call from this man, one of the outstanding citizens of Mont Laurier, and he complained about the brutality with which he had been dismissed by the mimic dictator who is in charge of the wartime prices and trade board operations in Montreal, a Mr. Robitaille. Mr. Pellerin came to Montreal, and we had an. interview with Mr. Robitaille when we were told that the investigator had been dismissed because he had taken out of the office at Mont Laurier, with the com-
[Mr. Gardiner. 1
plicity of the hon. member for Labelle, certain records and other confidential papers which were being used in my office. Needless to say, I deny emphatically this accusation, and I state from my place in this house that I never constituted this investigator my political agent in my riding, and that I never, either directly or indirectly, asked him to communicate to me any of the particulars pertaining to this office. I put the matter before the wartime prices and trade board, represented by Mr. Robitaille. Later, on February 7, 1943, I received a letter from Mr. Pellerin giving all the particulars of this incident. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall read this letter because it states the case much better than I could. It is in French and reads:
(Translation)
Mr. Maurice Lalonde, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Lalonde,
It will be three months on the 14th instant since I have been suspended, by telegram, from my duties as investigator for the prices board at the Mont Laurier office, and three months on the 28th, since I have been definitely discharged by Mr. L. C. Robitaille, although his letter did not reach me until December 2, 1942. I need not tell you that time hangs heavy on my hands.
As I have often told you, I shall always claim that I have been treated unfairly; that is why I asked you to take up my case and attempt, if possible, to have me reinstated by the competent authorities.
I renew my request to you and point out the succession of events as they really happened.
All through last summer, 1942, I received complaints from various Mont Laurier garage operators who claimed that the permits for the sale of tires, issued by Mr. J. A. Forget, local representative at Mont Laurier, were mostly in the name of the Laurin garage to the exclusion of other tire distributors of the district, i have often called Mr. Forget's attention to these complaints and in every case he answered that those who complained wrere nothing but jealous cry-babies.
Seeing that the complaints continued to come in and that, besides, I had had personal knowledge

I emphasize this phrase "personal knowledge."
-of a couple of infractions to the commission's orders on the part of Mr. Forget, I decided, while I was still in office, to find out whether there was any truth to the complaints received.
On November 12, while at my office, I asked the secretary, Miss L. Lamarche, to hand me the files relating to tire permits, which she did very willingly and without any comment. I then took a few notes, a copy of -which is in your possession. Under _ the circumstances, I thought I was perfectly justified in going over the files and taking notes, since serious charges had been made which I did not choose to submit to my superiors without further investigation. Moreover, I have never shown these

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
notes to anyone, not even to yourself, until the 2nd day of December, date on which I was discharged, and asked you to take up my ease.
However, on the afternoon of November 14, I received a telegram from Mr. Robitaille, suspending me from my duties.
As I had no inkling of the reasons for such a sudden action, I went to Montreal, on Sunday, November 15, and, on the next day, I saw Mr. Robitaille in his office.
It is then that I learnt from him that I was charged first, with being the political agent of the member of parliament for Labelle; second, with having secreted some files from the office and having taken them to your place on a certain afternoon, when we are supposed to have looked them over together; third, with having used a certain amount of pressure on Miss Lamarche or having attempted to intimidate her in some way in order to obtain the files relating to tire permits.
Needless to say that I have offered Mr. Robitaille a positive and energetic denial of these three charges; I even offered to swear an immediate written denial if he wished to call a superior court commissioner into his office. However, Mr. Robitaille did not comply with this request. I was the more at ease in denying these charges for the fact you were accused of being mixed up in this affair and that I was perfectly satisfied that you were in a position to support my statement.
S. Pellerin.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to add this:
(Text) If there were grave accusations against this man it was the duty of the district representative of the wartime prices and trade board in Montreal immediately to have a thorough investigation made to determine whether they were true or not. I offered Mr. Robitaille to file my own personal sworn affidavit, but he refused. My personal belief is that this Robitaille has gone too fast in this matter; I repeat again from my place in this house that all the accusations that I cited a few moments ago are false from one end to the other, and I ask the Minister of Finance to order a serious investigation by competent officers before whom, if necessary, I will appear and clear up the matter once and for all.
But, Mr. Chairman, there was another reason. There was a nigger in the woodpile.
Mr. GRAYDON; Just one?

Just one, and I think that is enough in the circumstances. This investigator was in the way of the manager. I understand that the specific charge which has been made against this representative that he was centralizing the tire sales permits in one garage has been investigated many -times. I can say immediately that I was not at all satisfied with the investigations carried on by the investigator of the wartime prices and trade board, because my own personal belief is that they did not go to the bottom of the matter.
Consequently I took the matter up with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who made an investigation and filed a report, but since as I am just a member of the house elected by the people of my district, I was not allowed to see that report. I can say, however-I think the minister is in possession of the report-that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police reported that the charge was well founded, that this garage man had his tires sales business increased by nearly 100 per cent and that the other garage man in the same locality dropped around seventy-five per cent. I cannot accept the explanations given by the officials of the wartime prices and trade board, explanations which are not satisfactory to any intelligent man who knows human nature. This specific charge has been found by the mounted police to be well founded and I really wonder why this man still occupies his position as representative of the wartime prices and trade board in my town.
One may say that the phenomenal increase of tire sales in one garage may be explained by the fact that this man has carried on a certain kind of propaganda or advertising, but I have before me a sworn affidavit by one of those people who complained about the matter in which this sale of tire permits was handled. This affidavit has been sent to the proper authorities, and it represents the real meaning of the gossip that one can hear around my district. It is because this man remains in his position, because the situation has not been straightened out, that one now hears around my district that the member is interested in the racket. I cannot stand for that, Mr. Chairman, and that is why I am on my feet to protest and say to the people of my riding and to this committee that that is false, that I am not interested either directly or indirectly in any kind of tire sales business in Mont Laurier, even if my tenant sells gas or tires or any kind of auto accessories.
This affidavit is also in French, but it throws a true light on the real situation that exists now in Mont Laurier. It reads:
(Translation) I, the undersigned, Alderic Desloges, merchant, of Mont Laurier, having duly taken the oath on the Holy Gospel, state as follows:
1.	At the -beginning of October, 1942, I made an application for tires at the garage of Mr. Gaston Forget;
2.	My application was delivered by myself in the office of the wartime prices and trade board, at Mr. A. Forget's, to himself, on the same day.
3.	About three weeks later, I went to see Mr. Forget in order to ascertain why I had not received the tires. He answered: "I cannot account for that." He then advised me to go
4404	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
to the garage of Mr. Yvan Laurin, and in fact he accompanied me there. After we had reached the garage he prepared a new application, which was left on the counter at the garage. Mr. Alphonse Forget then told me that everything was O.K. and that I would obtain the tires.
4.	About two weeks later, as a result of the application made at Mr. Laurin's, I obtained two 7.00 x 16 tires.
In witness whereof I have set my hand-
(Text) For the benefit of those who do not understand French, the affidavit I have just read1 is to the effect that this man has been directed by the representative of the office in Mont Laurier to buy his tires at a certain garage. Well, if this is to continue, I am asking myself if our people will have great confidence in this organization, and if I speak to-night on the matter I do not do so on political grounds, because the parties of whom I have spoken to-night are Liberals in good standing. If I protest against the treatment inflicted on Mr. Pellerin and on myself by this dictator, Robitaille of Montreal, it is because I believe, and I believe to-night as strongly as ever before, that the public interest is at stake, and I want in all sincerity that this board be honestly administered in my district. The board in some other fields has done a good job, and I am glad to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance upon that.
But this very special case is one of those that I cannot let pass without protesting as strongly as I can. This centralization of tire sales permits in just one garage man, and the conclusion of the report of the mounted police, together with the evidence I have filed before, is sufficient, I humbly submit, to justify the minister in taking this matter under his control; and in spite of certain advice that has been given by certain officials of the wartime prices and trade board, I say that the minister should dismiss immediately this representative from his position and place any other man there; I am entirely disinterested in who it may be, provided he is honest and capable.
There is also one accusation against this manager that has not yet been cleared up, and I think, although I am not quite sure of it, that the hon. minister has it on file. This representative is accused of having bought an inner tube without a permit from a certain garage man in Mont Laurier and having sold it to another party at the same price after having paid for it out of his own pocket. The evidence shown in this other charge is such as left me under the impression that this man, if he had done that, would have done something more, and that he does not deserve the position he now occupies.
I put these facts before the committee. I hope that the Minister of Finance will take

the necessary steps to remedy the situation. I again emphasize at this point that if I intervene in this matter, it is not on political grounds. I know the wartime prices and trade board has probably received instructions not to play politics, and I agree with that. If politics is to enter into the administration of these boards, we would rather cancel all these schemes and let the matter go. But if I had been interested in a political sense, I would not have put before the wartime prices and trade board any charge against my political friends. If I have done so, it is because it is a question of honour for me and for my family, because in my district gossip begins to circulate to the effect that "this man seems not to have the confidence of the people; yet being always in this position, it might be that the members may be interested in the racket." I emphatically deny that it is so, and my last remark is that I wonder how a man can stay in public life without clearing up this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a troublesome matter, this question of the fitness of Mr. J. L. Alphonse Forget to discharge the duties of representative of the wartime prices and trade board at Mont Laurier. The hon. member for Labelle is strongly of opinion that Mr. Forget is not a suitable representative of the board, and has asked for his dismissal, or, in the alternative, his transfer.
I have discussed this matter on two or three occasions with the hon. member for Labelle, and I have put a large amount of time on the case myself to see whether an investigation would reveal the existence of facts which would warrant the dismissal or transfer of this man.
With regard to the statement of the hon. member for Labelle that he was not privy to any examination of the files by Mr. Pellerin, who was dismissed, I believe at the instance of Mr. Robitaille, I of course accept without hesitation the hon. member's statement in that regard. It is, however, true that Mr. Pellerin examined the files and made certain copies, for purposes of his own, presumably, in the absence of Mr. Forget, who was in charge of the office; and Mr. Pellerin, if I understand the facts correctly, had not the authority to do so, his position not being such that he had the right to do that in the absence of his superior. At any rate the dismissal took place at the instance, I believe -the hon. member for Labelle will correct me if I am wrong-of the representative for the province of Quebec, Mr. Robitaille of Montreal.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
The crux of the charge or charges against Mr. Forget, because, after all, that is what I as minister am concerned with, is whether he was guilty of favouritism toward one of the garages. While the police investigation is confidential, I think it would do no harm for me to say that the member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who investigated the matter was of the opinion that there had been favouritism. On the other hand, a study of his report indicates that that opinion was a conclusion to which he came, and was not necessarily the conclusion to which everybody might come. It was in all respects an opinion, but it was based, I think entirely, upon the large proportion of sales in the district made by a certain garage known as the Garage Laurin, and I should add, upon the fact that sales of tires by that garage increased during 1942 and that sales of tires by the other garages in the town decreased during 1942.
Would the minister give the figures, if they are not confidential?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I can give the figures. I have not them in tabular form; I have a memorandum of my own, but I would have to go all through the police report, and it would take quite a long time. They would all lead to this conclusion, that there was a sharp increase in the sales of tires by the garage which was alleged to be favoured, and a sharp decrease in the sales of tires by the other five garages in the town.
If the minister will permit me, could he later on place those figures on the record?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have sent for another file, and I think I may have them.
Later on, maybe tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; I can get those. The investigator-I think he was the first investigator sent by the Montreal office to investigate the situation there-in his report to Mr. Robitaille on November 27, 1942, points out some fairly significant facts, facts which I think are a little difficult to answer. I will read this report:
Montreal, November 27, 1942. Mr. L. C. Robitaille,
Prices and Supply Representative,
Room 703, Aldred Building,
Montreal, Quebec.
Dear Sir,
A check-up of tire rationing in Mont Laurier reveals that 80 per cent of the applications made for tires or tubes were made by dealers in Mont Laurier. The balance-20 per cent-was made by dealers in the district outside of the town.
30 per cent of those applications were made by Garage Laurin.
17	per cent of those applications were made by Jean Brisebois.
10 per cent of those applications were made by Garage Vanchestein.
18	per cent of those applications were made by Garage Gaston Forget.
10 per cent of those applications were made by Grenier Frere.
10 per cent of those applications were made by W. Grenier.
Of the total applications made at Garage Laurin, 29 per cent were refused.
That is very important. If the percentage of refusals had been negligible for the garage which was alleged to be favoured, a much better case would be made, but it was not so.
At Brisebois, 19 per cent were refused.
At Vanchestein, 27J per cent were refused.
At Forget, 39J per cent were refused.
At Grenier Frere, 39 per cent were refused.
At W. Grenier, 53J per cent were refused.
As suggested, every tire dealer was asked if he could specify one case where one of his applications has been refused and that the applicant had obtained a permit by making his application through another dealer. Not one could be named although it -was rumoured. In the office, was one case of an application for tire and tube pending investigation as to the necessity of a new tube. In the meantime, a second application for a tire only came from another dealer for the same applicant. The latter one was granted and first one cancelled.
More details on separate reports for each dealer are given.
A report made by Mr. Pellerin on May 18, showing a deficit of 43 tubes in W. Grenier's place and never produced, is also attached.
Also found in Mr. Pellerin's desk were a few gas reports. These were turned in to Mr. L. Leroux for his inspection.
Yours truly,
E. Alphonse Lalonde.
"Forget".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; this is Lalonde, who, I assume, is Robitaille's investigator. That was the report of the investigator to Mr. Robitaille, made on November 27, 1942. Now, there has been investigation after investigation in this case; not only the police investigation, but repeated investigations, some of them taking a great many days, and involving interviews with large numbers of persons in the district. These reports have been studied, and the representative for the province of Quebec, Mr. Robitaille, stands very strongly by Forget. He states that as a result of the investigations Forget is in the clear, that there is nothing whatever which will justify his dismissal; and a review of the report by the wartime prices and trade board here, by the secretary and the general counsel and I think, perhaps, in a somewhat rapid manner by the chairman of the board, leads
4406	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
to the same conclusion, that there is not sufficient proof of anything against Forget which would warrant his dismissal. It must be remembered that there are a number of small incidents. The one mentioned to-night is perhaps the most serious of those minor incidents. It is that Forget himself, to oblige somebody, bought an inner tube for $2.74 or S2.76 and turned it over to his friend or acquaintance for that $2.76 without any permit being issued. Now, Forget has an explanation of that transaction which may or may not be creditable to him. It is that he was trying out the garage man to see whether he would sell without a permit.
He was an agent provocateur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And he did not pursue the matter any farther because it was a small one.
He was satisfying his curiosity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The transaction was a small one for which to dismiss an official, and in the opinion of the board it would be going a little too far. I have gone over the file, and the only accusation in substance against the man was one of favouritism, which certainly is strongly denied by all the board investigators who have gone into the matter. They say it can be readily explained on other grounds, and the explanation is that this garage had a good deal of what is called fleet business, and from the nature of its business it sold in the summer of 1942 a larger number of tires than the others.
The hon. member for Labelle feels strongly about this case. This man was appointed by the civil service commission. He is a civil servant, and he is entitled to retain his position unless he is proved to have been derelict in the discharge of his duties. Much as I should like to oblige a member of parliament, I do not think the hon. member for Labelle expects me to do so in a matter of this kind; and I must say that be never has, because he has recognized the fact that unless I had before me something that would justify the dismissal of this man I could not institute proceedings leading to his dismissal simply because the hon. member for Labelle feels that he ought to be dismissed and that he is not fit for the position.

During the course of the debate to-night some suggestion has been made about a recommendation either for the dismissal or for the transfer of this man. Who made that suggestion?
IMr. Ilaley,]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion with regard to his transfer was made on this basis. It was felt that the evidence did not justify dismissal, and certainly the trouble that has been caused in the community by persons taking one side or the other of this argument-and there are many who take the other side, for I have a petition signed by sixty-ffive residents of Mont Laurier urging that the man be not transferred-would seem to suggest that, the community being so divided, the man's usefulness is greatly impaired so far as that particular town is concerned, and that even if there were no clear evidence against him a transfer would be the sensible way of dealing with the matter.

It occurs to me that if the man is not competent; if he is not a proper person to fill the position which he now holds, it is clearly the duty of the department to dismiss him. If, on the other hand, he is fulfilling his duties in a competent, capable manner, and without any real cause for dismissal, then of course he should not be dismissed. You cannot have it both ways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But it may still be the sensible thing to transfer him.

That would be a matter of policy on the part of the department; nevertheless the department must take a more unequivocal position with reference to the question than simply saying to the man, "You are competent and capable, but we are going to get rid of you." That is what the hon. member apparently had in mind. I suggest that the department must make up its mind whether the man is capable and competent, there being nothing in particular against him so far as the department is concerned. If so, he should be retained; if that is not the case, he must be dismissed. The question of transfer is certainly at best a compromising of a rather peculiar situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The board is strongly of the opinion that the man is competent and should be retained where he is.

I thank the minister for the explanation he has given. May I point out that the civil service commission, in view of the reports of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, has refused to renew the man's certificate. He was hired on a yearly basis. At any rate, the certificate, if it has not been cancelled, was not renewed by the end of March of this year. I am not quite sure whether he receives his pay, but I can say that the treasury board is fully aware of the facts. In view of the opinion of the civil

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
service commission I am not alone in believing that this man is incompetent and should be dismissed.
Did my hon. friend not suggest that he should be transferred?

I made the suggestion to the proper authorities, because the matter has created a certain amount of uneasiness in my district with reference to the wartime prices and trade board, and everyone feels that we must go through this garage in order to have better tire sales bargains.
The hon. member is not being kind to the next one who is asked to take the man.

The minister has stated the explanation given by the wartime prices and trade board for the increase in these tire sales from, I believe, $7,000 to nearly S14.000, within a few months in just one small locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In one year.

In one year. The board states that this garage is the largest dealer in accessories and the customers are fleet operators. I know personally this is not true. That is simply an explanation to 'cover this man, and so long as the proper authorities have not decided to remedy the situation, either by dismissing the man or by transferring him, public opinion in my district will not be satisfied.

As I understand it, the
work of the wartime prices and trade board relates to two main functions, and I should like to say a few words about each of these functions. On the one hand, it is concerned with keeping prices down as far as possible, and, on the other, it is concerned with the supply of goods to the people of this country. In connection with the work of keeping down the cost-of-living index, I think hon. members of this house will agree with the spirit of what the minister said the other night when he spoke of the achievement of the board in that field during the course of this war, compared with what happened during the course of the last war. I say that quite definitely, because I shall be making some remarks with reference to figures that might suggest that that we do not appreciate what has been done. I do not wish to detract from that appreciation; nevertheless I think I should express the view which is commonly held by housewives, and by the husbands who provide the money for them to buy things with, that the cost-of-living index figures provided by the bureau of statistics, and referred to so 72537-279
frequently by the wartime prices and trade board, do not seem to be borne out by
experience.
The other evening the minister gave certain
figures which will be found at page 4254 of Hansard. I wish to refer to figures that have been given by the bureau of statistics, and perhaps if I use those that appear on page 70 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board it will be just as satisfactory. The reason I take the figures from the report rather than the figure the minister gave is that he gave just the final average, whereas the figures on page 70 of the report of the board give the final average, and also how it is made up, among several different lines of goods. In the third column of this report we are told that in the eighteen months from November, 1941, to March, 1943, the rise in the cost of living has been only -9 per cent. If I might compare that with the figure the minister gave the other night as reported at page 4254 of Hansard, I would point out that at that time he said there was a rise of 1-5 per cent in the period of eighteen months ending May 1 of this year. The minister will note that the figures in the table on page 70 break that down, and indicate that in the matter of foods, for one example, the increase in the period of sixteen months was 2-3 per cent.
I have in my hand a portion of the Winnipeg Free Press of June 9, which contains an article headed "City tests show 48-cent rise in Winnipeg's cost of living." May I add that this report arose out of an investigation made by the public welfare committee of the Winnipeg city council. The concern of that committee is with the standard of living of people on relief. In other words, their concern is not with a high or even an average standard of living, but with that of people under their jurisdiction. The paragraph I would read is as follows:
Cost of living in Winnipeg has risen 48 cents a month per person, buying tests recently conducted by the city public welfare department reveal. Test purchases in ten stores were made on March 23-
That is in the present year.
-and it was found that the average cost of a week's groceries for a family of five was $7.78. The same tests made June 1 disclosed that the average cost of a week's groceries for a family of five has risen to $8.38, an increase of 60 cents, or 7-71 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: During what period?

That increase of 7-71 per cent is in the period of ten weeks between March 23, 1943, and June 1, 1943. I do not wish to make any rash statements about the figures given by the dominion bureau of

4408	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
statistics, but I think the minister knows of the statements which are made throughout the country about those figures. There is a feeling that while the wartime prices and trade board have done a good job, as I have already said, compared with the experience of the last war, still people know by their experience and by methods of dead reckoning that the cost of living has gone up more than these figures indicate.
In connection with the ways in which the cost of living can go up, there are a few comments I should like to make. In the first place, owing to the fact that some lines of goods are off the market, it actually becomes necessary for people, in order to feed themselves at all, to buy in many instances a better quality of food than they would buy in normal times. People who normally look for bargains and are prepared to take second or third grades in order to balance their budgets, find that those second or third grades are not available. In many instances they are forced to buy better quality goods, with the result that the amount they have to spend increases.
On the other hand, in connection with some goods, such as clothing, the general feeling is that there has been a certain amount of deterioration in quality. While I realize, from an answer given some time ago at my request by the dominion bureau of statistics, that manufacturers are asked to take into consideration deterioration in quality, still the general feeling of people with whom I have talked is that in the matter of clothes people are not getting the same value for their money they were getting before the war. The result is that clothes have to be bought more often, and this fact reflects itself in an increase in the cost of living under war-time conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What did the hon. member say was the reason why people are buying better food?
I said that in many instances families which in normal times might in some lines buy second or third quality now find in war time that second and third grades are not available.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not?
I do not know why not. Does the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not because the very considerably improved income of the people causes them to buy better grades? Is that not, honestly, the truth? I think it is common knowledge that it is.

My view is that the better food some people are eating to-day is not

purchased by them because they want to spend that greater amount of money on it. It is purchased because the better quality is the only line of food available to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where is the rest of it?

I do not know, but it is not available. Another item I think the minister would have to take into consideration is the increase in taxation, part of which has actually gone into subsidizing prices and. in other words, really should be considered in computing the increase in the cost of living. I understand the dominion bureau of statistics feels it includes all the taxes it should in the cost of living index when it includes indirect taxes which show up in the prices people pay for food. But the bureau of statistics apparently does not take into consideration any of the direct taxes paid by the people of Canada. Yet those taxes have increased tremendously, and add to the cost of living. As I have said, part of the money paid in taxes is used-and I shall deal with that specifically in a moment-to subsidize prices. Part of what we pay in taxes is actually part of the price which we pay for some of our food.
Another factor which I think should be considered is that averages are very deceiving. It is one thing to find what the average cost of living is on certain quantities of goods across the country, and it is another thing to find a family which is at that precise average point. Conditions vary in different parts of the country, and they also vary considerably according to the income of the family. The dominion bureau of statistics can establish quantities of necessary commodities which it takes into consideration in making up its cost of living index, but whether or not the relative quantities of those various goods are bought depends upon the family income. Those in the lower income brackets do not buy the same proportion of all the various kinds of goods included in the list of things which make up the index. There are certain basic things they have to buy first, and so far as they are concerned if those basic things go up in price, then their cost of living index may have risen to a greater extent than is reflected in the average published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
One might ask why we are concerned with the figure the bureau of statistics publishes, and why we bring it to the attention of the wartime prices and trade board. The answer, of course, is quite clear; namely, that the cost of living bonus is paid-when it is paid-in proportion to the increase in the cost of living. Of course the wartime prices and trade

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
board watches the cost of living index closely, because that index indicates whether the board is doing its job, so far as the control of prices is concerned. I think there would be a good deal more satisfaction and perhaps a greater appreciation of the work of the board if the whole question of the determination of the cost of living index were gone into anew, in the light of war-time conditions, and in the light of some of the factors which I have suggested, and some other factors which no doubt other hon. members will suggest later on. This ought to be done to see if it is not possible to arrive at a figure which will more nearly approximate the experience of our people. I say again that that rise of only 2-3 per cent in the price of food in eighteen months hardly tallies with the experience of the housewives of Canada.
I have given as one piece of evidence on the other side the article in the Winnipeg Free Press, which is an account of a report made by an established committee in Winnipeg, and which shows that there was an increase of 7-71 per cent in the period of ten weeks ending June 1, 1943. When I started I said that I should like to make a few comments on the other side of the board's activities, namely, that of seeing to it that necessary goods are made available to our people. Here again I agree in spirit with the statement made by the minister the other night when he expressed satisfaction with the work the board has been doing in this connection. If all we have to suffer on this continent while this war is on is a few privations through not being able to get our chosen foods, that is not a very large price to pay and there should be no complaint so far as adults are concerned. I am going to take a moment or two, however, to speak on behalf of one group of citizens, our children and infants.
It seems to me that the board ought to do something to try to improve the situation with respect to the younger members of our community. We do not know how long the war will last, and what our children receive in their younger years may have a bearing upon their health throughout their whole lives. A great deal of progress has been made in recent years in the field of nutrition. We know the things that are necessary in order to build health, and yet some of the things necessary for infants and young children are most difficult to get at the present time. One item is the little tins of fruits which are prepared for children and which an adult would not eat unless he were ill. Then there is the good old stand-by, prunes, and there is also 72537-2791
canned milk. The minister made some comments about this the other night and pointed out that we have actually increased our production of canned milk. Despite that, shortages seem to be turning up. Corn syrup has become very important to babies, and then there are such things as oranges and other fruits.
I would suggest that some of these items be rationed. I know the minister said the other night that while it is realized that theoretically rationing is the most perfect method of distributing food, it is something to be avoided if possible.
