But despite all the difficulties that would be encountered, I think we should be concerned about the health of our future generation. The ration books indicate the age of the holders. Children under a certain age receive no coupons for tea and coffee, and I suggest that in reverse fashion it ought to be possible to make some of the things I have mentioned available only to our younger citizens. These items which are seldom found on the shelves of our stores should be made available on a ration basis. I know that a great many young mothers, and fathers too, are worried because they cannot get corn syrup, prunes and other articles of food required by small children.
I would refer also to fruits, such as oranges. Perhaps it might not be feasible to ration oranges, but I would suggest that the whole matter of subsidies should be handled with a view to making these commodities available to the younger section of our community. In this connection I would say that I have read with great interest certain parts of the report of the wartime prices and trade board. One section which I have studied quite closely is that dealing with the functions of the commodity prices stabilization corporation. It seems to me that too much of the initiative lies with the companies which are interested in obtaining subsidies and which make application to the corporation. I feel that the initiative should lie with the board. The board, after consultation with health and nutrition experts, should have a picture of what our children ought to have in the way of food. It should start first with the group to which I have referred and should take the initiative in granting subsidies in such a way as to make these things available to those who need them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman referred to a check in the rise in the cost of living made in Winnipeg and stated that the results of this survey indicated an increase in the cost of foods or groceries of 7-71 per cent between March 23 and June 1, 1943. From this he
4410	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
argues that the rise of 2-3 points indicated by the bureau of statistics for the sixteen months ending March, 1943, must be incorrect.

I was quite conscious of the fact that the periods were not the same. I had not the figures for the latter period and this was the best I could do. If it is true that there has been a rise of only 2-3 points in sixteen months, then I know that a rise of 7-71 points in ten weeks would have made the minister very much concerned and he would have done something about it. That much difference in the rate of rise would have been quite serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in position to express any views as to the validity of the Winnipeg survey. I do not know anything about it, nor do I know what foods they considered.

I can quote further from the article. It reads:
Foods tested were: bread, eggs (or one pound of liver), cheese, potatoes, root vegetables, cabbage, three tins of tomatoes, dried vegetables, dried or fresh fruit, rolled oats or cracked wheat, rice, tapioca (or barley), macaroni, flour, sugar, molasses, jam (or honey), salt pork or peanut butter, tea or coffee or cocoa, soap, salt, pepper, meat, shortening, butter or fish, milk.
When the tests were made June 1, the following increases were noted as against prices of March 23:	cabbage, increased from 15 to 44
cents; eggs, 34 to 38 cents; potatoes, 59 to 57 cents; root vegetables, 41 to 56 cents; dried or fresh fruit, 34 to 42 cents.
I would remind the minister that this survey was conducted by the public welfare committee which was considering whether they should increase the amount of the grant made to families on relief. In other words, they were thinking of that standard of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know anything about the weighting given to the various foods?

An attempt was made to find out the increase in the actual cost of living for a family of five on public welfare. As the minister knows, a committee of this kind would have had experience over a great many years with keeping down to a minimum the quantities of food necessary to keep a family alive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I say, I am not in position to argue one way or another about the validity of the survey or whether the correct weighting was given or the correct methods applied. That may or may not have been done.
I understand the same quantities were taken both times.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes; otherwise the comparison would be entirely useless. The position of the wartime prices and trade board with regard to the cost-of-living index is that it is an index compiled by another department of government, the bureau of statistics. It is said to be an excellent test of the real cost of living, but I suppose no index is perfect. I suppose opinions would differ as to the accuracy with which any index really indicates the cost of living, but compared with the indices in any country I know of I would express the opinion that the Canadian index is at least as good as any of them. It is true it may be said that in certain periods the index does not measure the true increase in the cost of living, such as in a very recent period when the cost of fruits and vegetables has gone up rapidly. The hon. member mentioned, for instance, an increase in cabbages from fifteen to forty-four cents. These would be imported fruits and vegetables, and there is no doubt there has been a great increase in prices in the United States. But these are not in the cost-of-living index. There are certain reasons why seasonal articles such as fruits and vegetables are deemed improper for inclusion in a cost-of-living index. There are certain vegetables in the cost-of-living index, but the great bulk of them are not there, and that causes some persons to complain of the cost-of-living index. The only fresh fruits and vegetables in the index are oranges, potatoes and onions. I understand that consideration is being given to ways and means of overcoming the technical difficulties of incorporating other items in the index. The chief technical difficulties are wide seasonal variations in prices, many fresh fruits and vegetables being on the market for only a few months of the year, wide variations in quality, and lack of standard units of sale. I am not in a position here to express any technical opinion as to the cost-of-living index except to say that it is generally regarded as a good index; the weighting is good and there is a wide but not too wide variety of articles included. Of course one of the most important items in the cost-of-living index is not food at all; it is rent. That bulks very large in the cost of living.

That is the reason I
took the table on page 70 of the report rather than the minister's figure which appears on Hansard, and made a comparison between the report in the Free Press and the actual increase for foods as set out in the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One of my officials points
out that twenty-nine cents out of the sixty

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
cents increase was for cabbages alone. There might be some answer to what I have said about cabbages; I do not know. It is a very difficult matter, one for statisticians to work out. There were tremendous increases in certain fruits and vegetables in that very period. That may be the reason for that apparently large increase, but certainly I would not regard that as prima facie evidence that the cost-of-living index is not a true index.

Before the minister deals with the other phase, may I say that the functions of the dominion bureau of statistics, including the cost-of-living index, date back, I take it, a good many years. It seems to me that with the emergence of the war and, in particular, this new function, namely, the control of prices by a board such as the wartime prices and trade board, it is certainly a debatable point whether the old basis of working out the cost-of-living index should be used. It was with that in mind that earlier this year I asked a question on the order paper which appears at page 2929 of Hansard. My question was:
Has the dominion bureau of statistics, since the outbreak of the present war, made any revisions in the method of determining the cost of living index?
The reply is quite lengthy, but I give this sentence from it:
No change in method has occurred since August, 1940. although two revisions in the index budget have been made.
My point is that what is required is not just revisions in the index budget, but an examination of the whole method in the light of this new economic phenomenon, namely, the attempt of the wartime prices and trade board to control prices. I appreciate the validity of the minister's argument. He speaks of the independence of the bureau of statistics from the wartime prices and trade board, and in one sense that is good, but it is also true that the wartime prices and trade board has an interest in the cost of living index because it indicates whether the work of the board is effective. My feeling is that these figures do not give the wartime prices and trade board a clear picture of its work. While its work is good; while it has achieved wonderful results in keeping the cost of living down, in my opinion it is not true to say that it has kept it down to an increase of only 2-3 per cent, with respect to food, in the period of the board's operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has made certain suggestions in the interests of children and infants. That gives me an opportunity of
pointing out something that has been done along those lines. We have subsidized all consumers in the purchase of milk. We have reduced the price of milk two cents a quart to all buyers in Canada. That certainly would be along the lines suggested by the hon. gentleman. He also mentioned oranges and orange juice. Similarly we selected oranges for subsidy. That is also along the lines suggested by the hon. gentleman.
To what extent was that done? Perhaps the minister would prefer to give the information when we come to the item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; I will get the figures. The board has also energetically sponsored the production of cod-liver oil in this country. It has taken great pains to assure an adequate supply of cod-liver oil.
With regard to tinned baby foods, I do not know just what they would be, but there are tinned baby foods, and the use of tin for these foods has been authorized to 100 per cent of its use in 1941. Of course the amount in glass containers, and so on, that can be manufactured is unlimited.

There would appear to be no shortage of tin in this connection; if the minister goes into any store in town he will find that there are certain infant foods of which there is an unlimited supply in tins. Spinach is one of them-Popeye must have had some influence there. But you simply cannot buy any children's tinned fruits in Ottawa anywhere, and it is practically the same in any other city. You cannot buy tinned peaches, tinned pears, tinned apricots- any fruit in tins.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is certainly not correct to say that there is an unlimited supply of tin.
I thought the minister said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I said that baby foods in tins could be manufactured to the extent of 100 per cent of the 1941 pack. The hon. gentleman was saying that the board should have some regard for the welfare of children, and I gave as an instance tinned baby foods. A very fine case can be made for what the board has done in that regard. I do not take any credit for it myself-
But it is only-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just a moment. The hon. gentleman does not give me a chance to get going at all. I was not quite clear as to what his suggestions were as to rationing, but I fathered that he thought certain articles not
4412	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
now rationed should be rationed. All I can say about that is that rationing presents such tremendous difficulties that if it can be avoided in almost anything it ought to be.

Might I say a word further. I appreciate what the board has done in the matter of tin, but I tried to point out that there is only a limited variety of goods available in tins. They happen to be all in the vegetable line. There are no fruits in tins. I imagine sugar has something to do with that. My point is that the boards should see to it that those things which are necessary-they can get the advice of nutrition experts-should, if possible, be produced and rationed among those with children of certain ages.
In connection with rationing I would suggest that it 'be done with prunes, with canned milk and with corn syrup. I happen to know that in some cities attempts have been made at voluntary rationing of syrup at the stores, at the suggestion of the local doctors. There are difficulties involved, but to me the importance is such that the difficulties are not insurmountable.

The matters which I have to bring before the minister to-night have to do with the recent beef orders and pork orders, and are raised on behalf of the British Columbia independent meat packers, who charge discrimination, and that the advice given to the wartime prices and trade board by and on behalf of eastern packers is to the disadvantage of the British Columbia independent meat packers, and so discriminates, generally speaking, against British Columbia.
The British Columbia independent meat packers have five members, whose offices and stores for business are in Vancouver. They made personal representation to me during the time I was at home at Easter. The names of the five are: The Pacific Meat Company Limited, Fletchers Limited, the Associated Packers Limited, H. Brown and Sons Limited, and the Alberta Meat Company.
The original beef order, they claim, divided Canada into fifteen different zones for marketing purposes and put a beef ceiling in each one of these zones. The beef order, however, did not take into full account the cost of shipping cattle from the prairie provinces to British Columbia.
Ontario and Quebec, generally speaking, do not bring any live cattle from the prairies for slaughtering on account of the long haul and the cost. These are bought by the packing companies, slaughtered in the provinces and then shipped east as beef.
[Mr. Ilsley.J
On February 6 a regulation was put into effect assisting beef shipments to eastern markets, completely ignoring the fact that British Columbia could not import live .cattle at the price differential set by the beef order.
There is only one cent a pound differential between Alberta and Vancouver price ceilings, which is not sufficient to cover the freight charges, handling charges and shrinkage. This one cent differential allows Alberta packers to pay more for their live stock than British Columbia packers can and so keep within the price ceilings.
Eastern concerns were allowed $1.35 per 100 pounds as a subsidy on dressed beef. This makes it possible for them to draw cattle from the Alberta market, kill these cattle at their Alberta plants in Alberta, and ship their beef east with the assistance of the government subsidy. The effect of this was to raise the cost of cattle in Alberta and Saskatchewan by retaining a strong demand on the Alberta market, but it has caused the independent meat packers of British Columbia to import and kill cattle at a loss or go out of business entirely.
British Columbia meat packers should be allowed $1.30 per hundredweight to equalize the cost and the selling price.
Every price order on hides or tallow or any other by-product is based on the supposition that the market for all these products is in eastern Canada. The ceiling price on these, generally speaking, are Toronto prices less the freight to western producers.
Under the order setting the prices for hides, tallow or by-products, hides are sold under two designations, namely, large and small packer hides. Large packer hides are priced at 25 cents per hundredweight more than small packer hides. Eastern officials and their advisers have classified the Canada Packers plant in Vancouver, who by the way have their head offices in the east, as a large packer, and the independent meat packers such as the Pacific Meat company are classified as small packers.
It should be noted in regard to this that the Canada Packers plant in Vancouver are killing about 1,000 head of cattle per month, for which they receive 25 cents per hundredweight more for the hides than the independent Pacific Meat company with no eastern head office but who kill approximately 1,500 head of cattle a month. Yet this independent meat company, classified as a small packer, are killing more than the company designated as a large packer, and to the advantage of the large company.
With regard to tallow, the price of tallow throughout the United States was set at a

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
nation-wide price, the same at any point of production. Canadian price ceilings were established with a 75-cent per hundredweight price differential between eastern and western points. All tallow is not processed in the east. Why should there be any difference in price?
With regard to pork and bacon products, here is the history. The history of the orders of the wartime prices and trade board and the bacon board as they affected British Columbia meat packers started in 1941. The packers at that date were allowed to kill for their domestic trade only the number of hogs slaughtered in 1940. The order was changed in July, 1941, when they were allowed to kill only 75 per cent of what they did in 1940. Then in November, 1942, this amount was again reduced to about 50 per cent of the number killed in 1940. There was a reason for this, because the number of hogs taken away from domestic slaughterings were added to the exports to the United Kingdom. No complaints were made regarding this, for it was realized that exports to Britain were very necessary, although it should be noted that the hogs taken away from the domestic market were handled by an eastern plant with a guaranteed profit. On two occasions the government has raised the price of export bacon, and this has brought about corresponding increases in the live hog market since 1941.
It has been urged that there should have been also a corresponding rise in domestic pork prices, but this is a matter which I am not arguing at the present time. I think, however, it should be stated that Mr. Peterson, director of live stock and poultry products, wrote to the independent meat packers in October last and told them that ceiling prices of domestic pork products are not out of line with current hog prices, admitting there may be exceptions in certain sections of Canada, including the Vancouver area, but that it was their intention to make some certain necessary adjustments. Although the price to the producer has advanced over $2 per hundredweight, the adjustments promised by Mr. Peterson have not yet been put into effect.
There are on the average 110,000 hogs marketed in Canada per week; of these, about
90.000	are handled by a handful of exporting firms who actually operate on these on a guaranteed government profit. This leaves about
20.000	hogs per week for slaughtering, and these 20,000 are divided among all the packers and pork processors throughout Canada, including the three exporting firms, who handle the 90,000.
On April 1 of this year order No. 247 regarding pork products was issued, and it is claimed
by the independent meat packers that this latest order is another attempt to put the Canadian packer industry into the hands of large eastern concerns. The features of this order, it is claimed, are discriminatory.
First of all, as regards the price set, the very basis for the pork order set-up is on pork carcases. Montreal and Toronto are allowed SI .50 spread between the cost price and the sales price, but the price differential allowed in Vancouver is only forty cents. Pork product number one of the pork order No. 247 carcase, with the head on, has a selling price in either Montreal or Toronto of nineteen cents or $19 per hundredweight, with a cost of seventeen cents delivered plus a shrinkage of * fifty cents from the hot to cold weight, making a total cost of $17.50 per hundredweight. That allows a spread of $1.50 per hundredweight. Vancouver has a selling price of eighteen cents or $18 per hundredweight, which is $1 per hundredweight less than the eastern price, and since the total latest cost in Vancouver is $17.60, it leaves a differential of only 40 cents per hundredweight compared with the $1.50 allowed the eastern packers. It is obvious by this that western conditions or interests were not kept in mind when the regulations were made.
Another matter. The price set-up of the pork cuts when the hog is broken down between east and west bears the same ratio to one another as do the carcases. Whilst it is relatively unimportant, it should be noted nevertheless that the cuts of pork must now be all put out according to the eastern style, a style which is quite different from what we have in British Columbia and from what we in British Columbia are and have been accustomed to, and bears out, I believe, the contention that British Columbia and the west were not at all consulted when these regulations were drawn up.
The claim is made by the independent meat packers that eastern concerns are being subsidized, that eastern concerns have the privileges on all by-products, and that eastern concerns have been allotted practically all hog slaughterings, leaving British Columbia with only 1,800 out of approximately 110,000 hogs which are slaughtered per week. Further than that they have been granted $1.50 per hundredweight spread in Toronto and Montreal to British Columbia; forty cents per hundredweight spread with an added disadvantage in British Columbia of being only allowed a meagre supply of hogs.
One further matter complained of is that in the prices set by the board for blood meal, British Columbia has been left out. In the

I realize, in bringing the matter to the minister's attention now, that he is perhaps not in a position at the moment to give me a definite answer to all the charges made by the independent meat packers of British Columbia, but I trust he has taken serious note of the charges made, because they claim they will go out of business and that then the three large companies, Swift's, Burns and Canada Packers will be in entire control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only say that the interests of the packers of British Columbia have been brought to the attention of the board by way of a brief or briefs containing the representations which the hon. gentleman has just made, and so. far as neglect of their interests is concerned, perhaps I might point out that the meats administrator is not an eastern man. Moreover, since about Easter, Mr. Diamond, the manager of the Pacific Meat company, has been a member of the advisory meat committee and is consulted frequently about the problems that arise. I wish for five or six minutes to discuss some of the principles in general of the administration of this particular department under the minister. It is unfortunate that this great question of control and of subsidies should come up ten or twelve days before the close of the session. Yes; I hope to see the session close by the end of next week. It would save a good deal of money to the country, because this parliament can do nothing. Our powers, privileges and functions have been taken away from us by various controls, sub-controls and bureaucrats, so much so that we might as well go home and leave the control of this particular work to the house of Gordon. It used to be that the parliament of Canada consisted of the House of Commons and the Senate; but ;hat is no longer so, because, as I say, all our privileges and functions have been wrested from us by a third house aforesaid, and we have little control over anything. We have practically no say in regard to any of the control policies of the government of the day. The cost of ceilings and subsidies and of administering this control system is 
$65,000,000, which is twice as much as the Tupper government spent in 1896, when they left office, to administer the affairs of the whole dominion at that time. I sympathize with the present Minister of Finance, because he has been bearing the brunt of a great deal of the burden of government. On general principles, I believe the public of Canada will commend the policy of trying to check inflation; but in trying to check inflation a great deal has been done that will have the opposite effect. There have been some excellent things, but the various boards have not adopted any cure, nor have they got rid of the disease; far from it, they are themselves causing inflation by unlimited, amateur price fixing, which is linked with wages.
We never knew how our mode of living was related to the far east until we lost command of the sea in the Pacific. Our entire way of life depended upon foreign products from the far east, such as rubber, gasoline, tea, sugar, coffee and many other imports, and we have had to change our manner of living in consequence of the changes that have been brought about by this war. No doubt the government was prompted to institute these various controls by what happened in the last war when prices went sky-high. But as Mr. Churchill said in the House of Commons on August 8, 1939, the people of Great Britain were obliged to look forward to a vast change in parliamentary government, in their method of government. It might seem a paradox, he said, that a war undertaken in the name of liberty should require as a necessary part of its process the surrender for the time being of so many of their dearly-loved liberties and rights. In the last few days, he said-he spoke, as I have said, in August, 1939-the British House of Commons had been voting dozens of bills handing over to the executive the most dearly-loved traditional liberties of the British people, but he trusted that those liberties would not be abused, that they would not be used for any class or party interest, but that the people would continue to cherish them; and he looked forward to the day, surely and confidently, when all those liberties and rights would be restored to them.
So far as we are concerned, I do not think it was ever intended that the control system, started with a skeleton staff largely made up of civil service staff, should go on expanding day by day until it reached the huge proportions we now see, going up in wage bills from $10,514,000 to $14,300,000 all in one year, just for administration purposes alone. This is a staggering thought for the taxpayer. The

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
minister must provide the necessary money by debt charges or by taking it out of the taxpayer by revenues and income. If this had as its object the winning of the war no one would object; but it can safely be said, so far as seventy per cent of i't is concerned, that it is not for the purpose of winning the war. It simply adds to the burden on the taxpayers of Canada, who have to pay income tax, sales tax and other war levies as well. In the last few days of the last session of parliament I asked what was the cost of this department of the minister, but I did not get a return until late in September. It is not his fault; he is overworked, I admit, and I am not criticizing either him or anyone else. The fact is, however, that we could not tell from day to day, from month to month, the number of people on the payroll of this enormous control system that we had. And if you got certain information to-day it would be changed next week. Now we have $14,000,000 for administration alone. The people are becoming bewildered at the cost of this institution. I asked last year what these ceilings involved, and the officials said, before the Easter recess, that they did not know. Then Mr. Gordon went to Winnipeg, and we were given to understand that the amount was $2,000,000. That information was given during the recess we had over the referendum. The government later, after the Easter recess, said the same thing; then the amount went up in the last fiscal year; and the cost of the Canadian subsidy programme from December 1, 1941, to March 31, 1943, has reached the enormous figure of $65,000,000. That, I repeat, is a staggering thought. If it were necessary to win the war it would be quite justifiable; but, as I say, a great deal of this is not necessary for that purpose.
If the policy of the government is to control all the activities of the people, to administer their affairs for them in every walk of life, from the cradle to the grave in this way, to control every man's business, whether retail or wholesale, indeed, to abolish all private business, private enterprise, thrift, and private ways of conducting business, then I say the people of Canada should know it. Many of the small storekeepers in our cities and towns have been driven out of business by this control system, and we in parliament have lost our control over the administration. We have simply handed over all our powers to an outside body to pass rules and regulations and by-laws and to send people to gaol and inflict upon them fines as high as $5,000. What a system! They would not have anything of this sort at Washington; they threw it out of the front door. Congress and the senate a
week ago simply refused to have anything tc do with it. The people over there are sick and tired of it all. They are willing to put up with a reasonable degree of restriction tc stop inflation, but the control that we have has destroyed all competitive business, both retail and wholesale, until private enterprise has been crippled, and no one any longer can conduct his own business.
What did they do in the mother country? They passed the Pre-War Trade Practices Act in 1942, which had the effect of putting the business man, large or small, back on the basis on which he operated before the war. I submit that the time has come in Canada for us to call a halt to the present tendency and to consider seriously where we are going. We are simply leading to more inflation by the policy we are pursuing. In addition to the personnel of the wartime prices and trade board and all their deputies in Ottawa, there are hordes of workers attached to the board outside, all over Canada a small standing army of busybody officials. Every day we read in the newspapers pages of advertisements announcing additions to this vast dictator system. There is an army of them, several regiments of them from one end of Canada to the other, every one of them making different, divergent announcements at the same time, until the people are bewildered. A morning newspaper in Ottawa has been criticizing them with reference to one commodity. The country is ready to stand some of this sort of thing, but to-day we have nothing but a modern tower of Babel in Canada, with these controls that do not control. Every city and town in the country are subject to the dictates of these controllers, sub-controllers and deputy sub-controllers, constituting one large army of officials. Not only that, but in the administration of the civil service departments we find some of the most able men in the country, who get only a certain amount of salary. Others, in these controls in this department are paid almost any amount, over the head of parliament, without our having anything to do about it. All the comptroller of the treasury does is to find out whether it is an amount paid as a war appropriation, under the war appropriation measure, and then just put his stamp on it. That is what he does, on sums up to $14,000,000. It is a fine system! The auditor general admitted to me in a letter last July, a copy of which I sent to the minister, that he has no control over expenditures made under the war appropriation bill. He has no control at all over that bill. That is under the control of the comptroller of the treasury.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
Anyone must know what will happen later, because I can say this that it will put a lot of men out of work, and that both before the war is over and after the war it will lead to wide unemployment if we do not check some of these unnecessary controls. What control have we over all these contracts which have been made by the board here? We have no control at all. We do not know whether the people are getting value for their money.
At this point I should like to read only a few paragraphs from the review by the National City Bank of New York. This is the June issue, for 1943, which deals with the economic results of Canada's whole ceiling and control system. In this issue it makes reference to a speech by the chairman of the board, Mr. Donald Gordon, delivered at Chicago. At that time Mr. Gordon spoke about subsidies, and the way in which they operated in Canada. I should like the committee to have the benefit of hearing what is set out in this review and, since it is not lengthy, I shall put it on record as follows:
Canadian subsidies are tied directly with regulation of profit margins on the particular product. They are designed to cover only a part of the increase in costs, and are conditioned upon adoption of various economies in production, importation and distribution. A good illustration of combination of subsidies with reduction of operating costs is provided in the case of leather footwear. This is described in an official report of the wartime prices and trade board, dated May 1, 1943, as follows:
"Soon after the maximum prices regulations were introduced it became apparent that the shoe manufacturers could not, until economies were introduced, carry on under the retail price ceiling. An investigation was carried out by the accounting administration and this indicated that approximately 15 per cent of the manufacturers' selling prices would have to be absorbed to enable the industry to carry on without serious difficulty, provided the cost of leather was maintained at prices prevailing during the basic period. It was arranged that 4 per cent would be passed on to the wholesale-retail group, that manufacturers would absorb 4 per cent, and that the commodity prices stabilization corporation would take care of the remainder by paying a temporary subsidy of 7 per cent. A simplification programme was initiated by the board and on July 1, 1942, the rate of subsidy was reduced to 4 per cent. The subsidy is not payable on footwear sold at higher prices than ceiling prices (e.g., sales to the Department of Munitions and Supply, and export), or on felt boots or rubber footwear."
The rate of Canadian subsidies is limited by various formulae and special arrangements. They are paid to low-cost producers at the same rate as to high-cost producers, but are considered income for tax purposes, and thus are recaptured in part when they result in excess profits.
In describing experience with the subsidies, the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. Donald Gordon, had this to say in a speech in Chicago in February:
[Mr. Church.)
"We have found, in practice, that it has not been necessary to pay out anything like the sums which some pessimists predicted when it was announced that subsidies would be payable under stipulated conditions. Moreover, we have found that our declared willingness to provide such subsidies has enabled us to enter into negotiations or discussions and to reach agreements between parties providing for a fair sharing of increased costs without actually paying a subsidy at all. We are satisfied that in many cases we could not have even arranged for necessary conversations if a willingness to subsidize in case of proven need had not heen expressed in advance."
The direct cost of the Canadian subsidy programme from December 1, 1941, to March 31, 1943, v'as about $65 millions, of which $34 millions was paid on imported commodities and $31 millions to domestic producers. The cost during the present fiscal j'ear may reach $90 to $100 millions. On a per capita basis, the equivalent cost in this country would be on the order of $1 billion.
Opinions as to the applicability of British and Canadian subsidy systems in the United States must take into consideration differences in conditions in the three countries. The British situation differs from ours in that a far greater percentage of commodities affecting British costs of living are imported and enter the country through relatively few ports, facilitating control by the Ministry of Food. In the United States the bulk of production is domestic; it is shared, even on the processing level, by many thousands of producers. Also problems of subsidies and price fixing in this country are more complex than in Canada, due to greater population and area and greater variety of production and trade.
That is their review. The people of this country are not satisfied when they see some of those who are engaged in this matter of control. For instance, let us consider the clothing industry. Was anyone brought to the control of that industry who knew anything about clothing, or simplified practices in it? Not that I know of. Why, they take a cut off here, a cuff off there, a sleeve off here. And what do men say who have been in the business all their lives? They say that if those controllers had stayed in the business to which they belonged, it would have been far better for the retail and wholesale clothing business. Some hon. members know, because I see some of them are wearing controlled clothing this evening. And that simplified process has been applied to all clothing, even to collars, shirts and ties.
I know something about control of this business. One or two of the controllers I know were not working in the clothing industry at all. All they knew about it was what they had themselves to buy from the retail store. Yet they are put over a great industry. That is a bad policy. In the city of Toronto, if one goes along Danforth avenue, Bloor street, St. Clair avenue or Yonge street and asks

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
any 'business man what he thinks about some of these laborious controls, he will say they are putting him out of business.
That is what we are heading for. I have seen something of the results of some of this inflation. Disaster will meet us in part in the end. Just wait until we see it next year. We are told that there will be $90,000,000 for the next fiscal year. Last year it was only $2,000,000. This year it went up to $60,000,000. Now we find in this review of the National City bank that it is to be $90,000,000 to $100,000,000.
Let us consider the coal industry, for instance. Some of these controllers put on seventy-five cents a ton for delivery charges, without the authority of parliament. That was one ceiling where something could have been done to help the poor retail man who has to deliver the coal. He could have been given that seventy-five cents out of a necessary ceiling, and it would have given him something on which he could exist and help get his retail coal delivered.
* In the United States they had an example of control before the war started, under what was known as the new deal. Not long ago I listened to a senator from Ohio, a former mayor of the city of Cleveland, who addressed a meeting in room 16 in this building. He was a republican, anti-new deal and isolationist. What did they do with the ceiling, pricefixing policy in the United States senate? I read the record of their debates and of congress debates every day, and I find that down there they have abandoned the new deal and this control subsidy system.
I am not asking for the complete abolition of control, but I am asking for some moderate reduction. I believe that in a country of only 10,000,000 or 11,000,000 people, some of this control may have merit. Credit should be given to the minister for much of what he has done to check inflation. But I plead with him now to let us reduce our tax rate, and surely this is one way 'n which it can be reduced. Let the retail man run his own business, and the wholesale man who knows his business run his own business for the remainder of the war with less state control, much of it unnecessary and not a war aid.
We have been at war four years. If during the next year, or during the remainder of this year and the year following we can relieve trade and business of some of these awful burdens and artificial barriers they have been carrying, it will be a blessing for the taxpayer and small business man. When we help the retail or wholesale man we are helping the taxpayer. It is all right to talk about this
72537-280i
subject in an academic way. For instance, references have been made to beef and butter this afternoon and evening. Instead of having somebody who knew something about beef and butter, either a farmer or a drover or a butcher, draw up some regulations with respect to these products, we find a teacher. Well, teachers are all right. We will remember that the Carpenter of Nazareth was a teacher. The average teacher is all right in his profession. But surely he should not start to run the grain business, or set himself up as an expert in the grain or any other business. Surely he is not an authority on retail gents' furnishings or ladies' underwear, nor would he be an authority on some of those other many things mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata with regard to some of the controls. Those matters are out of the teacher's sphere.
Let us have a more reasonable and a common-sense system of reasonable, necessary controls. People are getting sick and tired of many of these unnecessary controls. They are sick and tired of some of the bullying practices adopted by the board. We know that some people have been taken into police court, people who never were in courts in their lives before, and those people have had to pay fines, maybe up to $5,000 for some simple, unintentional infraction.
In conclusion, I plead with the minister that he should look into some of these matters, and try to cut down some of the controls by 30 or 40 per cent in the next fiscal year where they are found unnecessary, and so aid business.

There are just a few matters respecting which I should like to have some information from the minister. I believe in 1943 the retention of the price-ceiling policy and the prevention of further inflation will receive its greatest test. According to the information given recently, in 1943 the income of individuals as such will be some $400,000,000 more than it was in 1942, and there will be from $300,000,000 to $500,000,000 less civilian goods available during the year. All this points to one conclusion. Unless there is the strictest enforcement, aided by the cooperation of the Canadian people as a whole, inflation will progress by leaps and bounds during the present year. So far as the opposition is concerned, its attitude has been one of assistance to the government in preventing inflation. I have pointed out that in order to secure the Canadian people against the danger of inflation there must be cooperation on the part of the people as well as strict enforcement of the law against wrongdoers.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
The committee should have from the minister at this time a detailed statement of the number of investigations that have taken place during the past year into infractions of the regulations of the wartime prices board, as well as the number of prosecutions, province by province, that have taken place, the number of convictions registered, the fines that are being imposed and a general statement showing what is being done against these wrongdoers. Their number is increasing because there is not the enforcement of these regulations that there should be. Loyal and patriotic people accept the rigours of the regulations that are in effect; small business men are finding themselves in a position where they are unable to carry on, and, as times goes on, these conditions will be accelerated. They can be prevented only by strict enforcement.
The people as a whole feel that during the past few months there has not been the strict enforcement of the law that there should have been. As time goes on, there will be a greater incentive to commit offences against wartime prices regulations, and this will increase in proportion to the failure strictly to enforce the regulations in the courts. I should like the minister to furnish the committee with a full statement regarding enforcement to date, so that we may appreciate just what is being done to guard against the grave danger that now faces Canada through an increasing purchasing power and decreasing amounts of civilian goods. The people as a whole are cooperating; the wrongdoers are few in number, but they are increasing, and they will increase unless enforcement is made rigorous and drastic, unless penalties are increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether I
shall be able to cover all the ground mapped out for me by the hon. gentleman. He has asked for the number of investigations that have been instituted, but I am informed that it would be impossible to give that because there are so many. Investigations of complaints are taking place all the time. Some kind of record is kept, but it would not mean a great deal. A woman may complain that she has been overcharged, and the investigation into the complaint may take only half an hour. To make a list or to give the number of such complaints would not mean very much.
With regard to prosecutions, there have been 3,335 between December 1, 1941, and May 31, 1943. The ratio of convictions was ninety-four per cent. This number includes a certain number of prosecutions in con-
.
nection w7ith gasoline, tires and other matters, for the Department of Munitions and Supply. There were 467 gasoline prosecutions, 263 tire prosecutions and 63 others. I agree with the hon. gentleman that there must be enforcement of these regulations. If there had not been such a high degree of efficiency in the enforcement administration, perhaps our price control would have broken down. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) suggested the other night that most people in the country want to obey the regulations, but there is a minority who do not. If that minority is allowed to infringe the regulations with impunity, they become larger and larger all the time until eventually the whole structure crumbles. Some time ago I tabled the report of the wartime prices and trade board for the period September 3, 1939, to March 31, 1943. A great deal of pain was taken with preparing this report, and on pages 66 and 67 will be found a number of paragraphs on enforcement. It would take too much time to put these on Hansard, but the principles upon which the enforcement administration proceeds are set out in the report much more lucidly than I could set them out.
Does the minister think the prosecution of 3,300 people in sixteen months represents a serious endeavour to enforce the war-time regulations passed by this board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does not seem to me to be an insignificant number of prosecutions. The prosecutions have been increasing month by month, and perhaps I could give some figures
as follows:
October	 317
November	 303
December	   217
January	 332
February	 239

It never occurred to me that 433 prosecutions in a month was a small number. You cannot be prosecuting everybody all the time, and we are prosecuting quite a number.

I wonder how the Minister of Finance knows where he is at. Two speakers in the ranks of the official opposition have spoken within the last half hour or so. One of them upbraided the minister because of the extent of the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board and the way in which people were being interfered with, and then the other one rises in his place and upbraids the min-

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
ister because more people are not prosecuted and because the law is not enforced more rigidly. 1 agree with the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), that there must be a close check-up and control of prices. That is because of the increase in the amount of money in the hands of the buying public and the decrease in the consumers goods that are available.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that we are proceeding here without very much system. I had hoped to follow the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and refer to 6ome of the points raised by him, but now other matters have been brought in and I do not know just how we are to proceed.
The minister in his reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that he did not know how much validity there was in the figures he quoted in regard to the increase in the cost of living. I do not know whether the minister knows it, but I am satisfied that there are two or three million housewives in Canada who are doubtful about the validity of the figures that enter into the cost of living index. The minister would have to be more persuasive than he is in this house, though I am not finding fault with him on that score, to convince these women that the actual cost of living is truly represented by the cost of living index.
The minister also questioned whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave the proper weight to the various items in the cost of living index. It is difficult to give these items their proper weight. The weight given to them in the cost of living index is an average weight, but it is well known that the lower the income, the greater the proportion of it that must go for the purchase of food, and the increase in the cost of living has been more in foodstuffs than in perhaps any other one item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would not the larger proportion of the smaller income go for rent?

No; I do not think so, because if the income is very small, housing conditions are the first to suffer, if the family can find a cheaper place to move to. The important thing for the poor family is to ensure themselves enough food to at least keep away the pangs of hunger.
Then there is the point that fresh vegetables do not appear in the cost of living index. That is, I think, owing to the fact that the items that go into the cost of living index have not been changed for a number of years, not since 1913, I believe. There might have been revisions-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was all overhauled in 1940.

The overhauling was not so very extensive.
The minister also said that fresh vegetables were on the market for only a few weeks of the year. I know the minister is busy and has not the time to look into shop windows or go into stores to do any buying, but it is a fact that fresh vegetables to-day are a part of the family diet of everyone who can afford to buy them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that imported fresh vegetables are on the market only at certain seasons of the year.

Quite true, but some imported fresh vegetables are on the market for the larger part of the year. Head lettuce, for instance, from California is on the market in Vancouver for at least nine or ten months of the year, and so are quite a number of other vegetables. The Minister of Pensions and National Health takes considerable time to advertise correct diet charts and that sort of thing; but what is the use of wasting time and money in preparing correct diet charts telling people what to eat to have good health, and then to have a cost of living index which does not include these articles for healthy living, and to have wage rates which do not allow people to buy the things essential to keep them in good health. These are some of the matters to which the wartime prices and trade board, the Department of Labour and the Department of Trade and Commerce, under which the bureau of statistics functions, should give. consideration.
I do not care what the cost of living index says, because I know this: every woman who does the buying for her family knows that the cost of living is increasing continually, far more than is indicated by the cost of living index. I do not know how that increase can be stopped. I think it could have been stopped at the beginning if there had been posted up in each store a list of the prices of the main articles purchased. The housewife could then compare the price she was paying with the price on the list. Otherwise there is no proper check on prices, because no one can keep these prices in their heads all the time and know whether they paid less last week than they paid this week. They do know, however, that their pay cheques do not go as far this month as they did, say, two months ago. I bring these matters to the attention of the minister and point out to him and the government-because I do not know to what extent it comes under the minister's own department-that the cost of living as it bears

ft'or Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
on the low wage workers of this country is coming to the stage where there will be an explosion if something is not done about it.

There is another matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention. I have already brought it to the attention of his parliamentary assistant, but as with many other matters brought to the attention of the minister and his assistant, it goes to the department; the department gives an answer which the minister or his assistant brings back, and that is that. But we want something more sometimes than a stereotyped answer.
A standard price of 15i cents a pound has been set for honey all over Canada. It seems strange that some articles have a blanket price applicable from the Atlantic to the Pacific, while other articles, beef for instance, have price zones, and other articles, eggs, butter and pork, have different prices. But when it comes to honey there is one price, 15% cents a pound all over Canada. The honey producers of British Columbia had been receiving up until the war at least twenty cents a pound for all the honey produced in that province. I am not trying to get into an argument over why people prefer local honey to the imported article, but such is the case. It is the same with turkeys brought into British Columbia from Alberta and the prairie provinces. They are sold on the market at a lower price than turkeys and chickens raised in British Columbia because people prefer the local grown. We in British Columbia think we have a fine honey. The price which has been set, 15^ cents a pound, is 4% cents a pound below what the honey producers of British Columbia have been receiving for the last twenty years. I can say that of my own knowledge, because at one time I was in the honey business myself and kept upwards of 100 hives, so that I know what I am talking about. We sold our local honey around twenty cents a pound. I appeal to the minister; I say that we cannot produce honey there at 15i cents a pound. No one was kicking at the price of twenty cents. But the price was made 15% cents, and then to aggravate the situation we find that an inferior grade of honey is coming in from Mexico and is allowed to be sold at from thirty to thirty-five cents a pound. Naturally the local beekeeper wonders why his local good product is held down to the ceiling price of 15^ cents a pound, when in other years he got at least twenty cents for it, and honey from Mexico of an inferior grade is allowed to come in in large quantities-I understand it is coming in by the barrel-and is being sold at from thirty to thirty-five cents a pound.

What is the reason?
IMr. Maclnnis.]

I am trying to get the reason and I cannot find it. That is why I am raising the question in the house to-night, because when I brought the matter to the attention of the minister's parliamentary assistant I got a kind of answer, but my question was not answered fully. That aspect of it was not touched on. Now they are talking about changing a little the price of the pasteurized honey as against the unpasteurized. But I ask the minister why, when there was no injustice being done to the people of British Columbia, and no one was kicking, they should reduce the price to conform with the price of honey in eastern Canada. In Ontario the price was not, I believe, above 15i cents, because in years past quantities of honey came from Ontario at a much lower figure than that, as contrasted with the price of the local product. But when people want a local product and will pay for it, and it cannot be produced out there to sell at 15^ cents, I ask the minister to have the matter looked into further in the light of the representations I am making.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly will. I find it quite startling to be informed that the ceiling price is so much below the pre-war price. I do not know what the explanation is.
I should like to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will look that up.

Just one other question. Could the minister explain why canned salmon is one of the articles which is reckoned in the cost of living index. I am glad that it is, but I wonder why it has been chosen as one of the articles in this index, because it is not generally used. I believe that, generally speaking, there is more fresh fish used in Canada than there has been used of canned salmon.
There will not be two tins per family released this year-only 2,000,000 in all.
I wish the minister would explain why canned salmon is included, because last year very little wras sold1 in Canada; most of it went to Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only thing I can do is to make inquiry of my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have to repeat that the cost of living index is a product of the bureau of statistics; it is not a wartime prices and trade board index. It may be that an article not very widely used is an index

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
of the cost of articles which are more generally used. That occurs to me as possible, but I do not know whether that is the answer.

I wish to continue and to ask a few questions in regard to the matter of enforcement, which I think is of very great importance. The minister, when I asked the question a while ago, took the attitude that 3,300 prosecutions represented a not inconsiderable number of prosecutions for a period of fifteen or sixteen months. While the statistics which I intend to read at the moment are not very helpful and are not altogether comparable, the fact remains that in 1940, which is the last year for which information is available, there were convictions in Canada, for indictable offences, of 46,723, and for non-indictable offences, 456,109, or a total of approximately one-half million convictions during the year. Looking over the section of the report of the wartime prices and trade board to which the minister made reference, I find that there are 500 persons engaged in enforcement and investigational duties at regional offices throughout the dominion. Five hundred enforcement officers, in a period of approximately fifteen months, enforcing regulations that permeate through every sphere of life and have many ramifications, and a total of only 3,300 prosecutions, indicate, I submit, that there is not that serious enforcement of the regulations which there should be, having regard to the substantial increase in the cost of living which is taking place all over this country. As I read this section with respect to enforcement I find that, while there are the number of enforcement officers that I refer to, the major part of the responsibility of policing the price ceiling has been placed upon the women of Canada, so it states. Then it goes on to point out, at page 66, the method) whereby enforcement of the regulations is carried into effect, and it states that after an investigation has taken place-
A report is then made to the regional enforcement counsel, and if it appears that an offence may have been committed, the report is forwarded to the enforcement administration at Ottawa.
There are regional enforcement counsel in various districts in the dominion, and after the investigation takes place by the investigating officer, a report is made to the regional counsel. He in turn reports to the board itself at Ottawa. The report then states:
Prosecutions are undertaken only after a review of the case at Ottawa and only on authorization by the board; they are conducted in the regular courts by counsel appointed by the Minister of Justice.
I have not the exact figures at the moment, but some time ago I asked what was the total amount of fines levied in Canada up to approximately the 1st of March, if I remember rightly, and fines amounted to about $120,000, and counsel fees to over $50,000. In the enforcement of this legislation, $120,000 of fines imposed in a period of approximately, at that time, twelve or thirteen months, does not indicate the enforcement that there should be of these regulations. All of us admit the desirability of enforcing them; for, if infractions take place, as the minister points out, unless prosecutions take place and sure and swift punishment follows the commission of serious infractions, the whole basis will fall down on which the price ceiling is being built in so far as those people are concerned who are prepared to break the law and who have no regard to the necessities that the war demands.
I therefore wish to ask the minister, how many reports were received by the enforcement administration at Ottawa during the period he mentioned a while ago and, of the reports received, in how many cases did prosecutions take place? We have the latter information, but it does not indicate the degree to which enforcement is being made, unless we have a record showing the number of cases where the regional counsel have reported to the central board the necessity of prosecution taking place.
I want further information. So far as prices of food are concerned, on every hand one hears complaints. Prices are going up; prices far beyond those indicated by the index in so far as the increase is concerned are being charged. People have forgotten what prices were in September and October, 1941; they have no references as to them. They want to get the food; they want to get supplies, clothing and the like, and with the diminished supplies they are prepared to pay over and above what the price ceiling will permit, in order to secure possession of he goods. That is the one thing which these regulations are intended to prevent-to prevent the person who has surplus money from securing goods, such as clothing, food, that he would not be able to secure unless he paid a bonus to the vendor.
Therefore I wish, further, the minister to give this information; of the number of prosecutions which have taken place, how many related to prices, how many to rentals, how many to hoarding and1 rationing offences? The minister has a break-down for them; for as of the 31st of March, in this report a statement was given which indicated that up to

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
March, 1943, of the 1,679 prosecutions which were undertaken from July, 1942, 547 only related to prices, 730 to rentals, and 253 to hoarding and rationing offences. My experience has been that in so far as the rental regulations are concerned, enforcement has been reasonably strict, but in so far as food and clothing prices are concerned and infractions of the regulations with regard to them, there has not been a strict and sure enforcement.
While the comparison which I mentioned at the beginning-the number of offences, nonindictable and indictable, during the year 1940 -does not strictly show the position, it does indicate that, if a half million people were committing offences in Canada during the year 1940, many of them merely against statutes such as the offences against the war-time regulations would be, 3,300 prosecutions do not indicate that the enforcement officers are doing their duty. It says that the housewives of Canada are to be the policewomen, in the main, to enforce the law. I have already pointed out the weaknesses of that suggestion, with the number of investigators that there are, the number of officials that have been appointed to administer these regulations, my submission is that they should be engaged in the work of investigation. You cannot do it thoroughly, I realize; if you did, you would have a tremendous army of inspectors. But they can do at least this much, that when serious infractions are found, the penalties imposed shall not be the weak pusillanimous penalties that have been imposed up to the present time.
Let me give the record in that connection. At page 67 of the report we find the maximum penalty of $5,000 or two years' imprisonment or both. A penalty such as that is no deterrent to the wrongdoer when he knows that it will not be imposed. Let me quote from the report:
In the introductory stages of the price ceiling programme the courts were inclined to give light sentences for offences against the board's regulations. This tendency has not disappeared and fines still remain substantially lower than those levied for comparable offences in Great Britain. Sentences for most offences have been fines of less than $50, although recently a number of fines ranged from $100 to $1,000 for each offence. Several terms of imprisonment have been imposed for offences relating to rationing of rubber tires and gasoline.
My point is this: Laws unenforced bring the whole administration of the act into disrepute. Laws such as these regulations of the wartime prices and trade board, which are designed to increase Canada's war effort and to provide for the safety of us all, should be enforced by penalties that will act as a deterrent to potential wrongdoers. Penalties such 
as those one hears of imposed from day to day -$5, $10, $15 and costs-do not act as a deterrent to the type of wrongdoer that the wartime prices and trade board has to deal with, the type of person who in a time of war, for personal gain, endeavours to take advantage of the common peril of the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked me for a break-down of the prosecutions. Of the 3,335 prosecutions from December 1, 1941, to May 31, 1943, 894 were for infractions of the price regulations; 952 rentals, 465 rationing, 225 for "other" w-artime prices and trade board regulations.
What was the last?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were 225 other wartime prices and trade board regulations, 467 gasoline, 263 tires, 63 other, Department of Munitions and Supply, regulations. Then there were six other cases. These figures will add to 3,335. The hon. member asked for information as to the number of reports received from regional enforcement counsel. I have not that information here, but I will give it to the hon. member to-morrow.
With regard to the size of the fines, that is a matter over which, as the hon. member knows, the board has no control. It is a matter for the courts. I find, on looking over the list of fines imposed in the month of May, which is the latest month for which I have a report, that some were $500, some $250, some $200, some $100, some $50, some $25, some $15, some $10, some $5 and an odd one of $1.
Many of $1?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I had to look through several pages to find that one. It is a matter of judgment for the court as to what the fine should be. The court has the right to impose a fine up to $5,000. There were three fines of $500 each on one man for hoarding-
In Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I recommend to the Department of Justice-
What was he hoarding?
Wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Food and so on. I recommended that there be a remission, but I do not know what the Department of Justice did in the matter. I thought it was too much.
Did you ever ask them to jack up the dollar fines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I did not know there were any until to-night. They are for small offences. There is a wide variety of offences for which people are fined.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Boar A

In connection with enforcements, has consideration been given to the fixing of a minimum fine? As the situation is to-day, if a man in a district is brought before the local justice of the peace, naturally, things being what they are, the penalty will be a nominal one. Consideration should be given to the imposition of a minimum penalty, because the situation to-day is, in spite of the references that have been made to fines of $500, $200 and $100, that in the main the penalties are so small as not to amount to a deterrent to the wrongdoers.
There is another matter I would mention. We appoint outstanding counsel in all parts of Canada as regional enforcement counsel. The appointee in Saskatchewan is an outstanding lawyer who has given his services at a fee not in keeping with his abilities. He knows the local conditions. Why should his recommendation not be sufficient for a prosecution? Why should it be necessary for all cases from Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, and so on, after passing through the hands of the regional counsel, following investigation by trained investigators, be sent to Ottawa to be reconsidered? What is the purpose of that? In no other phase of prosecution is that course followed, except in so far as prosecutions under the Inland Revenue Act are concerned. Why is it necessary to get the consent of the authorities in Ottawa when the counsel in the province, the investigating officers, have noted infractions and have recommended that prosecution take place? Why should there be another board in Ottawa to determine whether the regional counsel in the province and the investigator have sufficient evidence upon which proceedings should take place? That in itself defeats one of the aims of criminal justice, namely, that punishment shall follow swiftly on the commission of the offence. Delays occur; witnesses disappear; conditions change by the time the prosecution is proceeded with, and where justice should be done it is not done. I should like the minister to explain the reason' for that precaution so far as this legislation is concerned.
Mr. 1LSLEY: The legal reason is that the order in council requires it; but the question I suppose really is, why does the order in council require it? I do not know that I have ever given much thought to that question, but it strikes me as being appropriate in some way or another. It may be that I am influenced by the traditional view. In the transaction of government business it has always been the custom that before a prosecution is instituted there must be authority from the appropriate governmental department headquarters in Ottawa.
But you already have a regional counsel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I know. But it is a serious thing to lay a charge against a man, and it is a question as to how much checking there should be. The hon. gentleman was not in the house the other night when the hon. member for New Westminster gave two . cases of prosecutions which he thought should never have been instituted. Those prosecutions were presumably reported to Ottawa by the regional enforcement counsel and were authorized from Ottawa, and it sounded to me as if one at least of them should not have been instituted. It was a .prosecution against an old age pensioner for some infraction of the price regulations, and it sounded to me as though whoever had authorized it had made a mistake. The hon. member may say that the board is just as likely to make a mistake as an enforcement counsel. But at least there is less likelihood of two making a mistake than there is of one making a mistake. That is, I presume, the reason why, generally speaking, we are cautious before instituting prosecutions. Somebody other than a local man has to pass upon it. The principles upon which prosecutions are instituted might become different in different provinces, depending upon the view enforcement counsel took. The hon. member may say that wherever there is a violation or wherever there is any infraction of the law, a prosecution should be undertaken. He may say that. Well, I do not think that would be the right thing to say. If he does not say it, then there must be a certain amount of discretion in the officials as to the class of the case or kind of case in which they will institute prosecutions. That is, the enforcement counsel must have sense enough to say, "Oh, that is a minor thing; it is really an insignificant case where a man has made a mistake. A warning is sufficient." If it were left to enforcement counsel throughout the country to exercise that discretion, it might not be uniformly or consistently exercised; and for that reason it probably is desirable to make it necessary to have authorization from the board at Ottawa.

Then what good purpose do these regional enforcement counsel fulfil? What is the purpose of paying them as much as $4,000 a year, if their recommendations mean nothing? There are local enforcement officials who investigate the infraction of the regulations. Why, then, have regional counsel? They have no position to fill, unless they are to enforce the law within their own province.
