Furthermore, I point out that these enforcement counsel draw salaries of $4,000 a year or more. Yet, when a prosecution takes place, they have nothing to do with it. The Department of Justice appoints counsel in the various cities and towns to attend to the various prosecutions, appointing them ad hoc for the prosecutions in question. If these ' regional counsel are not men who can exercise discretion, then they have nothing whatever to do, other than to supervise the enforcement of the law. If so, why have them at all, when they have no authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The enforcement counsel are really the head of investigational staffs. The investigators report to the enforcement counsel, and I presume that the enforcement counsel weed out certain reports, and say, "Do not bother with this one", or "We cannot get anywhere with that", and use their legal knowledge in so doing. They would recommend against a prosecution if it were apparent to them that there was no proof available, and they would realize, too, that they are dealing with laymen. Perhaps I am drawing on my imagination when I set out what they would do, but I believe I am correct. I think they would be discharging a useful function in so doing, because otherwise we would have all kind of reports coming in from 500 or 600 investigators, direct to Ottawa. I believe there would be a great advantage in having them gathered up, put into proper shape and winnowed out by these enforcement counsel.

I should like to ask one or two questions with respect to the situation in Ottawa. Some reference has been made to the various steps taken and. the various machinery existing for enforcement in connection with infraction of the wartime prices and trade board regulations in outlying centres and in the various provinces.
Would the minister give me some information as to what, if any, cases connected with infractions of the wartime prices and trade board regulations, during the period which has passed since the setting up of the board, have been referred to the Department of Justice in Ottawa? If so, how many of these cases have been prosecuted, after having been referred to Ottawa?
Then, to complete the picture set up by the hon. member for Lake Centre would the minister tell us how many of these cases, after having been referred to the Department of Justice, were then referred back to the wartime prices and trade board for further evidence, and how many were refused on the second submission to the Department of Justice, when the matter of prosecution was considered?

As I understand it, this raises an important question. The minister should explain to the committee whether or not the enforcement branch of the wartime prices and trade board has ever asked for its own final authority in connection with prosecutions arising from infractions of the wartime prices and trade board regulation. As the matter stands now, if my information is correct, final authority does not rest with the enforcement section of the board, but rather with the Department of Justice. What actually happens now is that the final authority rests with the Department of Justice. Not only have we regional counsel, and not only have we reference to the enforcement branch of the wartime prices and trade board, but the final authority does rest with the Department of Justice.
If that is so, I would ask the minister whether that has been working out, and whether it has been found to be a satisfactory solution to the matter of law enforcement. I would ask if it is not the minister's opinion that in so far as the enforcement section of the wartime prices and trade board is concerned, at least in certain cases there should be some final authority resting in their hands. I would ask for this information, because I believe it goes to the root of the peculiar position in which the enforcement branch actually finds itself at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will get the information, but I shall be very much surprised if I do not find that the correct answer is that the wartime prices and trade board has the final authority to authorize prosecutions and does not refer these matters to the Department of Justice at all.
I have asked for the number of cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will find that out. They apply to the Minister of Justice to appoint counsel to conduct prosecutions. But, by law, the right to make a decision as to whether a prosecution shall be authorized or not rests with the wartime prices and trade board.
And not with the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am fairly sure that is correct, but I shall obtain definite information on the point.
Perhaps the minister does not wish to commit himself. I am inclined to think he will find a different answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.

Does the minister think the fines have not been severe enough? Is it his impression that the law has been enforced properly?

Privilege-Mr. Lacombe

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should not like to express an opinion on the point. I shall discuss the matter with Mr. McGregor, the enforcement administrator, and after having done so, I can make a more intelligent reply.
Mr. BLACKM0RE: I am inclined to think the hon. member for Lake Centre overemphasized this matter. I do not believe that members of parliament should urge that the minister apply fines more severe than are now being applied. If the law is being kept, that is sufficient.
If the law is being kept, we do not need to worry about the fines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the point. The test of the efficacy of the law is not the size of the fines. A perfect condition would be where no prosecutions would be necessary. One might find a situation where the control was perfect, and where there would be no prosecutions whatever.

Does the minister
think we have arrived at that stage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I do not think so. I
know there are certain, infractions of price regulations; there is no doubt about that. There are a tremendous number of prosecutions, and I believe the number is increasing.
Not if it applies to farmers.

It is my impression
that, considering the almost bewildering complexity of the regulations under the control of the wartime prices and trade board, the infractions of the law are surprisingly few.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The rentals regulations are
pretty well observed, and the number of prosecutions there is on the down grade.

In that connection,
would any prosecution be instituted without authority from the central board in respect of rental cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
None whatever?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; there must be approval from Ottawa.

I have a very peculiar case I should like to bring to the minister's attention to-morrow.
